Under the provisions of the Company's Act the authorised works may be carried out in sections. and the work will be proceeded with either as a whole or in section, as the Mee- tors shall, in the interests of the Shareholders deem desirable. The Central Section comprises the intended line .between Chesterfield anti. Lincoln, This portion will be about 52 miles in length and for the greater part of its course will pass ,over ' the Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire Coal Measures. The -works on this section are in course of construction, and under' the Contracts are to be completed within three-and-a-half. Tears. Advantageous alliances have been made between this Corn- pany and the Great Eastern Railway Company and the Great Northern Railway Company respectively, for the develop- ment a traffic over the intended lines of this Company in con, neation with the lines of each of those Companies. The Great Eastern Rail. ay Company have also, upon, certain terms, after -mentioned, undertaken to subscribe. £250,000 in this Company's Capital. The Directors have, amongst them, applied for 20,000 Shares which will be allotted to them in full at par. None of the Company's Capital has been underwritten upon commission.

div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

WitsT does the enthusiastic girl say to her soldier lover? "You ar-my chap." THE belle of a "lumber district," in speaking of a disappointed beau, said, "lie looked as chop - fallen as a tree that had just been cut down." THE iille son of a rich man being told by his physisian that he must be more moderate in his diet, exclaimed : "Why, rve llvsd ou imp ever since I was born :"

TWO REASONS. Two reasons are given both equally good, Why the credit of Henry's so bad— _ for naying he has :not the means if he would, Nor is he inclined if he had. El IT is a standing rule in my church," said one clergyman to another, "for the sexton to w ake .up any man that he sees asleep." " I think, replied the other, "that it would be better for the sexton, whenever a man goes to sleep under your preach- ing, to wake you up !" "My boys and girls are growing so fast, I don't know what to do with them 1" said a mother tO,her bachelor brother. "liter me 1" he exclaimed. " What I becoming iast, while still so young 1 Alas I for the future of our country I" and he went out, leaving the mother in a sad state of mys- tification. SAID a miserly old man to his wife: "Don't you think that our George is making his sweetheart rather too costly presents?" "Oh, well," responded the wife, with meaning emphasis, "he'll probably be stingy enough after they 're married to make amends for his genellbsity now." "SEE here 1" exclaimed a,-couceited fop, who was always retailing stale jokes, "these scientific chaps say the world is half a billion years old I Come now; isn't that making it rather aged?" "Not near so old as some of your jokes,". quietly an- swered a companion. "I DON'T HIM my church so much as you sup- pose," said a lady to iier minister, who called on h, er during her ittne-s ; "for I make Betsy sit at the window as soon as the bells begin to chime, and she tells me who are going to church, and whether they have got on anything new." `! WELL, Sinipsou, I'm glad to see you back. Hope you made big money out of your show." "I did at first, hut lost it all in Texas." " Why, how so?" "On account of that confounded mummy in our collection. The coroner would insist upon holding an inquest over it in every town we stopped' at. It cost me 50 dole. for fees every time." " Wuzez are past going, John?" asked an Austin woman'of her husband, with whose relatives she was not on a very friendly footing. "I am going to call on my folks," he replied; "but is this coat not rather shabby ?" "Yes,", replied the wife, turning up her nose, "but as long as you don't go among decent people it is good enough." " WHAT'S an audiphone ?" asked an ignoramus of an acquaintanee ; who replied: "It is a con- trivance for making a deaf person to hear by placing a sort of telegraphic communication on the teeth." "Humph !If was the response. "Enables deaf folks to hear through their teeth, hey? Then I a'pose it 'll enable blind folks to see through their eye teeth. hey ? " A MUSICIAN was once seeing the sights at Donny- brook fair, wileu he was attracted by the sound of a very loud violin in a tent: He entered, and said to the player, "My good friend, do you play by note ? " "Nicer a note, sir." "Do you play by ear, then?" " Niver an ear, your honour." "How doY 0 u play, then?" "By main strength, be jabers !" "Au I" said an old Highland piper, as he was describing to his comrades at home his recent experience in Edinburgh—" Ali I there was a'e nicht 1 'll ne'et forget. There were eighteen pipers besides mese in Mrs. Glass's wee back parlour in the Coogate, and we were a' playin' at the same time an' a' playin' different tunes, an' I jist thocht I was floatia' to Heaven." DANIEL WEBSTER was once dining with a snobbish Bostonian, who had the ill manners to boast of the quality, age, and cost of his wine. He even went ineo a computation of the interest on the cost that accrued since the purchase of the wine. Webster listened courteously, and when the computation was ended, he held out his glass to his host and quietly remarked: "Let us atop that accumulation of interest." " When I was once in danger from a tiger," said an old East India veteran, "I tried sitting down and staring at him, as I had no weapon." How did it work?" eagerly asked a bystander. "Per- fectly ; the tiger didn't even oiler to touch me." " Strange ! very strange! How do you account for it?" "Well, aotnem;rnea -thous, was because I sat down on a high bra.ncL tall tree." VERY POOR.—A gentleman once asked a little girl, an only child, how many sisters she had, and was told "three or four." Ber mother asked Mary, when they were alone, what induced her to tell each an untruth. " Why, mamma," cried Mary, "I didn't want him to think you were so poor that you hadn't but one child. Wouldn't he thought we were drefful poor?" Me grandmother (ays Mark Boyd) once awoke , my grandfather in the middle of the night, and told him that she much feared their son Willie, who slept next room to them, had become deranged, as she had been listening to him for some time speaking loudly and rapidly to himself. Her husband listened, and came to the same conclusion; and they forthwith hurried to tneir boy's bed-room to know what was the matter. Willie's explana- tion was that, as they were going to the seaside next day, he wished to save time, and was saying his prayers over and over to last him during the holidays. Tow CAMPBELL once told an amusing story of an accident that had happened to him in a small country inn when travelling in Scotland. He had been stopped by the weather in the afternoon, had dined, and indulged himself with a toothpick to wile away the idle after-hour. Enter chamber- maid—Sir, if ye please, are ye dune with the toothpick Why do you ask? I suppose I may pick away as long as I like ?" "Oh, dear, na, sir, for it belongs to the Club, and they hae been met amaist an hour I" The disgust with which the instrument was thrown away may be more readily imagined than described. A HIGHLAND DONALD oas tried for a capital offence, and had a rather narrow escape; but the jury found him "not guilty." Whereupon the Judge, in discharging, thought fit to admonish him. " Prisoner ! before you leave the bar, let me give you a piece of advice. You have got off this time, but if ever you come before me again, I'll be caution (surety) you'll be hanged." "Thank you, my Lord," answered Donald; "thank you for your good advice; and as I'm na ungratefu , I beg to gie your Lordship a piece of advice in return. Never be caution for ony body, for the cautioner has often to pay the penalty." THERE is a good anecdote told of the little town of Portland, Indiana. While a certain steamboat was "putting out" from there not long since, for New Orleans, the mate, an old boatman turned to some passengers and remarked—" This little town, gentlemen, looks dull, but I tell you it is perhaps a mighty brisk place. About fifteen years ago, as I was going down with a flat boat to New Orleans, we stopped here to procure some provisions. I went up into the town, and, seeing a coat hanging out of a shop-door, just took it. The owner came after me, took me before a magistrate; I was tried, convicted, took thirty-nine lashes, and was back to the boat in fifteen minutes! I tell you, gentlemen, a mighty brisk little place is that same Portland. "Is there any one distinctive trait or function possessed, by man exclusively ?" asked Professor X., Lafayette College, Easton' U.S., of the members of the sophomore class. "Yes, air, he talks." "So does the parrot." "He walks erect," quickly responded another. "So do the chimpanzee and kangaroo." "He thinks, reasons." "So it is believed do horses and other animals." "He loves, hates." "Faculties given to God's lowest as well as highest creatures." "He weeps," said a big- headed youth who had not spoken heretofore. " Ah," exclaimed the professor, rubbing his hands, "I think ,you have it. He weeps." •So does a mule, sir,' said a slow boy at the foot of the class. "A mule ?" "Yes, sir," answered the boy; "I was reading only to-day about the weather being so cold that the muleteers were nearly frozen on the tow-path of the canal." AN old lady, hearing of fire escapes, said she thought it a very good idea to give a fire a chance to escape from a building: "and then," she added, "if it doesn't escape, why put it out. without ceremony."

div.p: LANCASIIIRE ANECDOTES.
Me following anecdotes of East Lancashire life are culled from a paper read by Mr. Thomas Nor- bigging before the member of the Manchester Literary Society :

. To .the introductiou of water and steam power ' matlinery.in the earlier part of the century, there was' no stronger or more bitter opponents than the Rossendale folks. In the earlier days, in many of the larger houses wereshand machipes for the card- ing, spinning.and weaving of woollen, whilst nearly every-oue of the smaller houses had its hand-loom; and when the factory system began to be introduced into the district, and water power was employed in turnirg the machinery, the strong prejudices of the inhabitants found vent in :the form of a prayer, which, in seasons of droughfran thus: " The Lord send rain to till the ground, , But not to turn the engines round."

-- Same as yo, Meister George," has become a classic saying, It thus originated: The occasion was the eleetion of a poor-law guardian—an exciting event when political parties, Whig.and Tory, broUght out their candidates, and put fdrth their atiength, in the contests Political feeling ran high then as now, and guardians were elected on the colour of their politics, quite independently, of their special fitness for the position. George Hargreaves, Esq. J.P., was the ruling Tory spirit in the heart of leossen- dale talley in bygone years—i man'o the staunchest integrity and blameless life, but Tory to tile back- bone. The voters, many of whom were dependent on him in various ways, because he was &man of property and an employer alabour, were Crowding into the school-room to record their votes, George himself marshalling his partizans and scanning the faces of doubtful supporters. "Who are you voting foi. Sam ?" shouted out Mr. H. to a steady Rossen- dentin, elbowing his way among the crowd. ' Same as yo, M aister George.' with a nod "same as yo," and Maister George answered back with a grateful smile. So it is "same as yo," Maister George," when the opinions of any present day political or other weak-backed inhabitant are in question.

A number of stories are told of Mr. John Brooks of Sunnyside. Sam Brooks, the well-known Man- chester banker, and John were brothers. The family came originally from Whalley. One of the stories I have not seen recorded in print, and it is too good to be lost. When government by a municipality was first introduced into Manchester, it is said that' John Brooks was asked to stand as a town council- lor or alderman, but being doubtful as to the expediency of taking such a step, he promised to consult with his brother Sam and be guided by his odvice. Accordingly lie spoke to Sam on the sub- ject, informing him that he had been asked to take office as a new-fangled town councilor. What did he think of it? Would it be wise for him to agree to the request ?" " Will they pay you for it?" enquired. Sammy, with a quick interrogative glance at his brother. "0, no 1" John replied—" there'll be no pay for th' job—nothing for it but the honour of the position." "Humph 1" responded Sammy, "honour be hanged ; let me gi'e thee a bit of advice John: Whenever thou does ought for nought, do.it for Otte sell

Reverting again to hand-loom days, and stepp- ing over by Tharneyford and Tooter Hill, the high ridges separating Rossendale from the Todmorden Valley. by way of Dalesgate (where Waugh assisted at the poker weighing), we may encounter some • of the finest examples of Lancashire and Yorkshire border character, . their conversation overllciwing with mother wit and ready repartee. One old dame recounted the straggles ot poor folk in the days when there was plenty of law but a sad lack of justice dealt out to the workers, and.,described the kind of men and their servant i that held the noses of the poor to ,the grindstone, whilst they themselves were. laying the foundation of big fortune. It wur hard wark thoose days, I con tell thee to get porritch and skim milk twice a day, wi' happen a bit e bacon on Sundays. I remember once I had to go fro' near to Stoodley Pike across Langtield Moor Wl' my cuts. It war a raw cowd morning, very early, before it war gradely leet, an' when I geet to th' taker-in—eh ! and 'they were hard 'uns were thoose takers-in— he says, • Are you here so soon, Betty? Wurnt you all fley'd o' :meeting th' deil this soon, Betty? Wurnt you all fley'd o' meeting the deil this morn- ing as you coom across Langfield Moor?' I said, • Nowt a' th' sooart ; 1 wur noan foart 6' meeting th' deli uo o' th' moor, for I knew th' hangments

In one of the hamlets lying beyond Todmorden in the Burnley Valley, there was a curious speoithen of the Lancashire border character, Hiram Fielden, who kept a grocer's shop, and dealt also inf other commodities expected to be enquired for by a vil- lage community. In his younger days Hiram had been a cotton weaver in a mill, but his ambition was to save a bit of money; get married, and open a "Badger's shop." By the exercise of great frugality, along with the help of the savings which his wife, Betty, brought him, he achieved his purpose. He began business in a humble way at first, but gradu- ally as his customers increased, his business grew, and instead of continuing to , vend treacle from a two-gallon can, he at length ventured on giving an order for a whole hogshead at once. The arrival of this consignment created quite a sensation in the village; the like had never been seen before, and the urchins who watched the un- loading of the precious cask, and saw it safely, desposited end up in the corner of the store, smacked their lips as their imagination pictured the luscious reservoir of sweets. In the course of the day a further con-ignment, this time of white- wash brushes, arrived, and Betty mounting a chair in the corner, and thence stepping on to the treacle barrel, was just in the act of hanging the brushes on a hook in the ceiling, when the barrel end gave way beneath her, and down she flopped up to the armpits in the syrupy mass. Hiram, who was busy at the back of the snop, hearing the crash, hurried in to ascertain the cause, and stood; for .a few moments gazing in consternation at 'thehead of his better half, barely visible above the barrel edge. What was to lie done? Ruin and disgrace and ridicule stared him in the face! but with great presnce of mind he ran to the shot) door, closed it, s.lot the bolt, and then drew down the window blind, Mounting on the barrel,and securing a footing on its edge, he succeeded by the help of a clothes line Ihe looped on to the hook overhead, and which she stoutly grasped, in gradually extricating Betty from her savoury bath. Carefully he stroked the treacle from her as she rose ceiling-wards, and, that no 105....0f the merchandise might ensue,at the same time wiping her down with a cloth dipped in a bucket of water, and thus all traces of Betty's mis- adventure were soon obliterated, and nobody but themselves any the wiser. , Hiram, in recounting the circumstance to me, confidently, after long years had elapsed, declared that the run on that hogshead of treacle was immense. -It was relished by his cus- tomers, old and young, and Its delicate flavour was the occasion of more oatmeal being consumed in

the village than had ever been prievously known se that what appeared to Hiram to be an irretriev- able misfortune turned out profitable in more ways than one. " Eh! but mon,' said Hiram, shaking, his head, and with a solemn countenance " that hogshead o' treacle wurt' ruination o' me ! " " Ru- ination ! " I exclaimed, in puzzled suprise, " how do you mean?" " Well,'Yo' aft, me an' eawr Betty had been wed for three years, lin' up to then we'd no childer, but boo began fro that time forrud an' II never stopped till boo had thirteen ! Eh I that barrel o' treacle were t' ruination o' me I" I

But, like not a few of the Coast Railway Railway will be to Warrington ? Then, let railway undertakings, the Lane hi make a journey to the ancient Derbyshire town East Coast Railway owes it Chesterfield, which is famed for its crooked church needs of a great coal' spire, and which lies about midway on the route of- .oXlsting raocomockty the new railway. He will find that, though "as The' this new • mile- crow flies" Chesterfield,is, comparatively speaking, shire and not a great distance from Warrington, as the rail- pert of ' ways at present run It is a circuitous and a much- ee delayed journey. Then let him forecast what will l' be the modus operandi of getting within view of the crbcked spire, say, in June 1895, when it is ex- pected the new line will be opened. He will then wend his way in a leisurely manner—tfor dis- creet railway travellers are never in ,a, hurry— over the bridge at Warrington, and on getting near the present grounds of the Football Club, he will enter,the handsome new railway station—it will be handsome for this Company does all its business in a handsome way—take a ticket 'from the civil booking clerk—all booking clerks ;are civil—and then enter his train which will 'no doubt start punctually to time. The train will pass through a pleasant country in the Grappenhall and High Leg!' direction and on to quiet Knuteford, of May Queen repute, and on again to Macclesfield—what is Macclesfield -renowned for ?—thence to Buxton, world-famed for its medicinal waters, its Pool's Cavern and its Devonshire Hospital, and on again through ~the fine hilly Peak country by way of Bakeweli and Calver to 'Chesterfield. This will be about as direct a route as any railway traveller could wish to travel, and the directness of the route is continued right on through Tuxford, Lincoln, and Alford to Sutton-on-the-Sea, at which there is to be a harbour and dock. From this it will be seen that the new railway will give Warrington a direct and easy access to parts of the country which ate at present comparatively difficult to get to, and as a censequence it must be a convenience to all who travel by rail, and a source of profit to the traders and manutacturers of the district. The first sod of this new railway was cut on Tuesday, at Chesterfield by Mrs. Wm. Arkwright, of Sutton Scarsdale, and, in common with a large number of other press representatives from all parts of the intended route, I had the pleasure of witnessing the interesting ceremony. As I have said, the present way to Chesterfield is a circuitoes one, but on Tuesday there was an additional cause of delay. Yorkshire was enjoying the holidays, and the fine weather seemed to have drawn the "Tykes" out in unlimited numbers. From Warrington 'to Penistone, through Stockport, the ride, was of the usual description, though one could not but admire the beautiful summer garb which the whole stretch of country has put on. At Penistone we came within the holiday-making area. A change of. trains Was here made, and we set out with a large contingent of passengers for Sheffield. Another change at the cutlery town nut us fairly on the road for Chesterfield. The 'distance now to be travelled was not great, but a respectable propor- tion of time was taken to travel it-in: We drew up at every waygde station, and every station added its quota of passengers, to be stowed away in al- ready overcrowded carriages, till by the time our destination was reached, every available sitting and standing space was packed. Chesterfield was en fete tor the occasion. The church bells were ringing out merry peals, and the crooked spire was ornamented with banners. Huge poles carrying flags and festoons were set up in the streets, and the blare of brass instruments and,' the shriller sounds of the fife were to be heard from several dir- ections. Visitors had evidently been pouring into the town all the morning and the streets, which are not of the widest,were crowded. In passing through the town one noticed that the inhabitants testified their good wishes by numerous mottoes, eipedesing hopes for the success of the Cross Country Riflway and big dividends for the shareholders. "Success to the East to West— Of railway schemes it is the best." Such was one of the inscriptions, and it will be seen from this that poets do not grow at Chesterfield. The "cutting of the sod" took place just at the outskirts of the town, at a place called Maynard's Meadow. Here a large marquee had been erected, and it was under the, grateful shade of this that the 'ceremony was performed. A distinguished company had assembled. Amongst many others were the Duke and Duchess of Newcastle, the
man)

party,the Master Cutler of Sheffield,and many local dignitaries. So far as I could see, Warrington was represented only by Alderman Francomb and Mr. R. A. Naylor. The local volunteers were drawn up along one side of the , marquee, and the band discourse i music.from an elevation at the front. Mrs. Ark wright performed her part in a graceful manner. With a beautiful spade of black ebony, elaborately mounted with silver, she litted.a few sods intO3 handsomely designed wheelbarrow, which she then wheeled along a short platform covered with baize and at the end tippet the sods over the side, and, putting herself "between the stilts" wheeled the barrow back again. The spade bore this inscription : " Presented to Mrs. William Arkwright, of Sutton Scarsdale, by the directors of the Lancashire, Derbyshire and East Coast Railipay Company, upon the occasion of her cutting the first sod of t'hat railway at Chesterfield, on the 7th of June, 1892." Both the spade and the wheelbarrow were, after the opening ceremony, presented to Mrs. Arkwright by the Duke of Newcastle. Mrs. Arkwright then made a neat little speech in which she said she felt grateful and flattered in having to take so important a part in the day's ceremony. Perhaps, however, her qualification was that she had taken so keen an interest in the scheme from the begin- ning, an interest begun when the scheme was simply an idea in the brains of one or two, but which had grown and grown, keeping pace with its triumphant progress through Parliament, and which, she trusted, might attend iti henceforth during the construction of the line, and she should not be satisfied until she had travelled from Chesterfield right across England from the East- Coast to the West Coast, on the embodiment of the original idea. That event, she predicted would take place within three years, and she invited them all to accompany her on the 7th June 1895. Cheers were then given for the East to West Railway, and the band played while the corapany dispersed. A banquet was afterwards partaken of at the Stephen- son Memorial Hall, at which there was a large number of invited guests present,and at which toasts were proposed and responded to by, amongst others, Mr. Arkwright, who was in the chair, Sir William Leng, Mr. W. Bromley Davenport, M.P., Sir Ben- jamin Baker, Mr. A. Barnes, M.P., Sir Henry Watson, Mr. Moberley Bell, and the Mayor of Chesterfield. This account of the inaugural ceremony of a railway project which is bound to have very vital results for Warrington amongst other places, may be fittingly closed with a recapitulation of a few of the salient features of the scheme itself. The railway will stretch from War- rington.to Sutton-on-the-Sea on the East Coast, and will consist of a double main line of the best. 'construction. At Warrington the railway will be in close proximity to the Ship Canal docks, and at Sutton a sum a £700,000 is to be expended in establishing an East Coast Dock. The total length of line is 174 miles made up as follows : Main line, Warrington to Sutton. 1304 ; branch, Mac- clesfield to Heaton Mersey,9f; do. Langwith to Beighton, 11±; do. °Berton to Newark. ; short junction lines, ; colliery branches, 6; total, 174. The finance of the railway Wines Out in round figures as follows :—Estimate for land and works—Main line and branches to Beighton and Cheadle 8u1me,£5,250,000; branch from (Merton to Newark, £250,000; dock. £700,000: rolling stock (at the rats of 15,00) per mile) £875,000 ; add for cost of Act (£150,000), interest on capital during construction, administration, and con- tingencies,2l,42s,ooo , total in round figures,£7,soo,ooo. Coming to the probable earnings of the company, and basing the calculation on the average earnings of lines of similar geographical position, an average of £6,165 per mile has been arrived at. Making a liberal deduc- tion for working expenses-53 per cent.—£6.l6s would yield 61 per cent, on a total capital of 71 millions. When the matter was before Parliament it was said to be the most important railway undertaking ever sanc- tioned by the two Houses in a single bill. Over a hun- dred petitions ware presented in iss favour,and it passed without a single mile of its line being struck out or a Soaps, single pound of its capital being refused. •

The full prospectus of the Company will be found in our adyertiz,ing columns. It will be seen that the Board of Directors includes the Duke of Newcastle, the Right Hon. Earl Mauners, Lord Francis Pelham Clinton Llope, Mr. Wm. Arkwright, (ex-high Sheriff of Derbyshire), Major F. B. Dalrymple, and other highly reputable gentlemen. With regard to the sources of general traffic import traffic, both on the Mersey and at Sutton, and transit through there between America on the one hand, and the Northern European Ports on the other may be confidently looked for. The machinery and wire, the leather, soap and glass of Warrington ; the salt and chemicals of the Cheshire salt district ; the silk or Macclesfield ; the lime-stone of the Derbyshire hills ; the milk and cheese of the dairy districts

MR. BRUNNER, -M.P., ON STATE PENSIONS.

On Whit Monday morning Mrs. Brunner, wife of Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., for North vrich Division, performed the ceremony of unfurling the new banner of the Upper Mersey Watermen and Porters Association, in Devonshire Square, Runcorn. After- wards Mr. Brunner delivered a brief address to those around him, who could hear his voice, several thousands having assembled. That morning's cere- mony, he said would be another of the many ties which bound him to Runcorn, and he described the banner as an emblem of many, many years honest loving work for the employes of Runcorn—it was an illustration of the work that had Wen done by men in Friendly Societies throughout Great Britain and Ireland for generations past. (Hear, hear.) There had of late years—and it was a matter for their most careful consideration—been an attempt to do what seemed to him to be equal to asking them to abandon the good rules and efforts made in the past, and to induce them not to rely upon them- selves, but upon State-aid. One proposal after another had been made by men whose names filled people's mouths, to induce them to accept, in place of the work that hall been done by that and kindred societies, a pittance of a miserable and paltry ss. per week, after they had attained 65 years ot age. He asked them to maintain their self-reliance, to stand by their friendly societies, and tur:er as long as they lived accept charity at the hands of the State instead of the honest results of their work and self-reliance. (Applause.) He could not understand how anyone could hold up to man, as an ideal to be aimed at, the miserable idea of ss. a week upon which to be independent. Ile asked the ladies to strengthen their husband's arms, to stiffen their backs, and to insist that it should be friendly societies and manly self-reliance upon which they should depend, and not the State pension. Mi.Brun- ner explained that the scheme provided that work- men before they reached 25 years of age should save £5, to which the State should add a bonus of £l5. The .£2O to be placed in a savings bank, and the workman to contribute .£1 a year until he reached 65 years of age, when he would receive a pension of ss. a week for life. That was the scheme put forward for their acceptance, and he should not hesitate as time went on to recommend to his fellow countrymen that they should not be content with it, that they should not accept it • but rather that they should proceed on their old lines, and maintain their Friendly Societies, for thereby they would do better than accept the ss. per week. There were a great many workmen in England Who agreed with that view, which had been thus admir- ably expressed in a Trades Unionist paper, which had unfortunately come to an end : Say, Joe, my lad, you're awful kind 'Bu t this 'ere pension job, To go and aggravate your mind To get us this five bob. And if you'll kindly let us know, In spite of Harcourt's sniggers, How much we've got to pay,dear Joe— You've such a head for figures! Your plan, as I construe it, is That we saves up five pound, You then puts fifteen to it, Just to make it twenty round. But then again we must begin, Oh! Joseph, naughty, naughty, To pay our bloomin' thick 'uns in Till they reach five and forty! And when worn out by sore abuse We reaches sixty-five, The poor old slave is no more use In the industrial hive. To keep us from the Worklioase. Or being hauled before the beak, You werry kindly offers us Our own five bob a week. Well, Joe, its werry kind of you To go tO so much trouble, But listen, Joe, I tell ysiu true, We're going to burst he bubble And, Joe, you'll see 'fore very long— That is if you're alive— We'll do the blootnin' Contisong Before we're sixty-five.

He trusted that the future of Friendly Societies would be happy and prosperous, that they would proceed on their beneficent course, and that they would rejoice in the results of their work. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Gatley (the secretary), proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Brunner for having so gracefully unfurled the banner. The motion was seconded by Mr. Banner, and carried with cheers. Mr. Brunner responded. He said it was still the custom fore man to speak for his wife. Some day they would learn better, they would be put in their right place, the ladies would speak for them. (Laughter.) He was an unregenerate man in that particular, and had the impudence and audacity to reply on behalf of his wife. They had been charmed, their hearts had been warmed to see that great assembly, and they would look hack upon that as a red-letter day in their, lives, to have been with them on that lovely June morning.
ALDERMAN lIIRRISON ON DRUNKENNESS.
CORRESPONDENCE WITH THE TEAPERANCE FEDERATION • AND MR. E. J. GUEST, J.P.
The following correspondence ha l arisen out of the extraordinary remarks which Alderman Harri- son made on the subject of drunkenness in the Warrington Police Court, on the 23rd May :

Warrington, June 3rd, 1892. Warrington Temperance Federation, Alderman Jos. Harrison, J.P., Dear Sir, I have been requested by our Executive Corn- mittee to convey to you the accompanying resolution which was unanimously passed at the largely attended meeting held last evening at the Elorsemarket-st., Cocoa Rooms, under the chairmanship of the Rev. J. J. Longhorn, M.A.:—"That this meeting of the Committee of the Warrington Temperance Federation strongly pro- tests against the language used by Alderman Harrison, a magistrate of the borough of Warrington,in the Borough Police Court, on the 23rd of May, regarding it as cal- culated to defeat the ends of justice by discouraging the Chief Constable, and the members of the police force in the execution of their duty." I am, Dear Sir, Yours truly, WM. RC BERTS, Hon. Secretary.

The principal ma-tiers in the minutes of the General Purposes Committee were resolutions referring to the proposal to provide a new concert hall for the town, the Ship Canal. &c., all of which have previously appeared in our columns.

He was of opinion that that resolution would be agreeable to the Council—(no, no)—especially when they read the array of improvements the General Purposes Committee appeared to contemplate carrying out before very long. It was clear that whenever those improvements took place a very large sum of money would be required, and that sum could not be spent without materially increasing the rates of the borough, He thought that, as representatives of the ratepayers. they ought to be extremely careful in the way they went about those improvements. div.head: Warrington, 4th July, 1892.
div.p: Warrington, 4th July, 1892.
Mr. W. Roberts. Dear sir, Ibe to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 3rd instant, enclosing ;copy of a resolution alleged to have been unanimously passed by the Committee of

the "yarrington:Temperance Federation," strongly pro- testing against the language used by me as a magistrate of the Borough of Warrington, at the Borough Police Court on the 23rd of May, regarding it, as calculated to defeat the ends of justice, by discouraging the Cnief Constable and the members of the police force in the execution of their duty." May I trouble you to point out to me, the language to which they take exception, for I certainly never in- tended anything of the kind, nor has a re-perusal of my remarks convinced me, that I did on the occasion referred to, Use language calculated to lead to such result, as the members of the said Committee seem to anticipate. I remain dear sir, Yours faithfully, J. HARRISON, Warrington, June 7th, 1832.
Alderman J. Harrison, J.P. Dear Sir,— Your letter of the 4th inst. to hand.

You ask me on behalf of the Committee of the Tem- perance Federation to point out the language Le which they take exception. I may at once state that the impression created upon the minds of the Committee was, that the whole of your remarks from beginning to end were calculated to dis- courage the police in prosecuting publicans for permit- ting drunkenness, and that, instead of any magistrate placing the slightest obstacle in the way of the Chief Constable and his officers by discouraging their efforts, the difficulties the police have to contend with should be recognised as well as those of the publican. The fact that it rarely happens that a publican is fined in War- rington and that drunkenness is rampant amongst us is unmistakable evidence to any impartial mind that the police must be encouraged to do their duty without fear or favour, and if our magistrates will not do theirs we will not be satisfied until we have magistrates upon the Bench whose chief desire will b 3 to help by every means in their power, and not hinder those who are seeking to remove the reproach which through drunken- ness has so long disgraced our town. I am, dear sir, Yours faithfully, WILLIAM ROBERTS. Hon. Secretary, Warrington Temperance Federation. 8, Woodbine-terrace, Latchford, 7th June, 1892.
W. Roberts, Esq. Dar Sir,

_ In reply to yours of this day's date, in which you decline t 3 comply with my request, that you shout I point out the precise language used by me at the Borough Court, to which the "Warrington Temperance Federation," takes'exception, I am, I consider, relieved thereby, from the responsibility of saying more than this, that as my letters of the 2nd and the Tch instant, addressed to Mr. E. J. Guest (which you say you intend by his authority to publish in the local newspapers) cover all that I wish to say, or think it necessary to say, I will spare both you and myself the necessity for any further controversy in the matter, but as you are the accredited representative of so respectable and influen- tial an organisation as the " Warrington Temperance Federation," presided over by an esteemed clergyman of the Church of England, I should like to add, that while I regard drunkenness as a "baleful vice," I find it im- possible not to sympathise with those who are doing their best to lessen the evil ; still, zeal and prudence do not always go together. The fact is, the "Public House" is the "Poor man's club," and as such, we must think twice, before we close the doors at such houses, against those for whose use they have been set apart from time immemorial, unless we can put something better in their place. It is a fallacy to regard public-houses as merely places where drink is consumed. Eatables are also dis- pensed there, and they are the only places where food can be obtained for payment on the Sabbath, and those who are independent of them, and who are surrounded with all kinds of home comforts and luxuries should, I think, not take ato circumscribed and selfish view of this question. Sunday is the workingman's holiday, and particularly when away from home, in pursuit of pleasure or recrea- tion, it would be extremely hard and irritating to ex- clude him from the use of a respectable well-conducted public-house. And to those who have no other means of social communion, such houses are a positive boon for they enable men to inform their ignorance, and to devise all sorts of measures for individual,local, and even national advantage, which friendly and intelligent inter- course between man and man, is almost sure to promote. Believe me to remain Yours faithfully, J. HARRISON. Warrington, June, 8, 1892.
Alderman Jos. Harrison, J.P. Dear Sir,—

, Your letter of the 7th inst. to hand, and in reply I quite agree with you that it is unnecessary to carry the correspondence any further, especially after the opinions you express in your last letter. As you do not object, I
have handed the le'ters, including your corresTonclen,e with Mr. Guest, to the Press. 1 a in, Dear Sir, Yours U.ithrutiv. W. ROBERTS. Hon. Secretary, Warrington Ternperan:o r ederation.
CORRESPONDENCE wurii MR. E. J. GUEST, J.P. Oak Mount, flelsby, Warrington, ISt. June, 1892. - -

Jos. Harrison, Esq., J.P. My Dear Sir, It was only only on Tuesday that I heard of the remarks you made in the court on the subject of drunken- ness. Seeing that most of tne sad cases that come before us are due to this cause. I think it is the duty of every magistrate to lessen this evil by encouraging the police to watch with the utmost vigilance the conduct of those to whom licenses are granted. Your remarks, I fear, will discourage this vigilance, and will tend to make the police utterly careless as to the conduct of publicans and their assistants. As to the necessity of public houses, you and I doubtless widely differ; but I trust we agree in wishing the people to be sober. Publicans can, if they will, guard against the vice of intemperance by refusing to supply liquor to those who have already had enough. Tho signs of approaching drunkenness cannot be mistaken by those who are careful to observe them. ' and the time to refuse to supply liquor is long before a man has ceased to care what he does or to know what he is doing. I know that the financial interests of the publican will lead him to be unobservant, hence the wisdom of giving power to the police to prosecute those who are more careful of their own than of the public advantage. Though I doubt the true wisdom of the publican who prefers ill-got money to morality, as magistrates we are only adrninisterers of the law and not legislators. Permit me to say, I think you will, on reflection, see the justice of my brief criticism of your recent remarks. _ . _ _

div.head: Yours faithfully, E. P GUEST.
div.p: Yours faithfully, E. P GUEST.
6, Woodbine Terrace, Latchford, June 2nd, 1892.

My dear sir, Permit me to thank you very much for the copy of the " Alliance News," which you were good enough to send to me, containing a somewhat pungent criticism upon some remarks, I am charged with making, at the Borough Court a few days ago, apropos of a charge of drunkenness preferred against two young women and : the landlord of a " Public House " in Bridge-st. , I should indeed be very sorry, I may say grieved, if I thought, that the remarks I made, should or could have the effect of diminishing the vigilance with which the police are in my opinion, bound to watch all the public houses in the town, with the view of suppressing as far as possible the sin of drunkenness, the accom- panying evils of which, can hardly be exagoerated ; and upon this question, I am sure there would be no appreciable difference of opinion, betwedn 113, thoug,h there might be, as to the best means by which such a happy result might be accomplished, and with our opinions, I am led to believe, the great majority of Inn Keepers would agree, for drunkenness it cannot be their interest to encourage in the face of the stringent condi- tions with which the renewal of licenses are granted. If the writer of the article in the " Alliance News," had been in Court during the hearing of the case, to which he has so elaborately devoted his attention, I am of opinion that he would have spared himself the trouble of criticising with such a wealth of expletives, : what he WAS pleased to Cali my definitions of drunken- ness &c., the truth being, they were not iny definitions at all. They were simply quoted by me, and which I have either read or heard of somewhere, but the paternity of which I am unable to fix. I allule to these involving the subtle distinctioni, between" intoxication" and " drunken- ness," and they were jocularly given by me, in reply to an " Inebriate," who was unduly and impu- dently pressing one of the Police Officers for an explanation of what he meant, when be said his interrogator WAS drunk on the pre- vious night. They were not my definitions, nor my serious opinions, which I should have thought any discriminating person might have perceived. But what I do seriously maintain is that the same conclusive evidence should be insisted on, in support of a charge made against a publican as well as against any accused person, whether he or she (as the case may be) is a " Publican," a" Baker," a " Tailor," or a " Shoemaker" but in the case of a " Publican," my experience leads me to say, that it has been the fashion very frequently, to draw unjust inferences of guilt, and to invest them with all the weight of direct and unimpeachable evidence and made admissible for the purpose of procuring a con- viction, and this very case, I submit, is an illustrative one. The sin of the magistrate was it appears to me one of omission. They oinitted to convict the publican of an offence, which it was not proved lie had commit- red. Mr. Hunt might well say, " That in future he would be most particular, how he summoned anyone again for a silititur offence." km )et tAnyay and appropriate utterance, for assuredly, sufficient particularity had , not been observed in this case. Let the facts speak for I themselves ! The conviction of the young women for being drunk, was a " condition precedent" to the conviction of the publican, yet it failed hopelessly, Mr. Hunt having called only one witness, to corroborate the statement of the police officer, and instead of doing so, to my great surprise, he point blank refused to swear, that in his opinion, the young women were drunk, although he had been close to them, and watching them fora considerable time, and this witness, was corrobo- rated in his opinion, by several other apparently respect- able persons. It is as you know, a sound maxim of English law, that if any doubt exists, as to the guilt of any accused person, he or she (as the case may be) is entitled to the benefit of that doubt, and therefore the.admonition that I presumed to give was a very necessary one to the effect that the greatest caution should be exercised, and the most indisputable evidence of guilt or connivance should be given, as the necessary preliminary to a con- viction in a case where the consequences might he so ex- ceptionally serious, as in that of a publican whose very livelihood might be imperilled thereby. 1 Permit me to thank you for your -frank and friendly criticism, which, I assure you, is received by me in the same good spirit is which I am sure you meant it. Believe me to remain, dear Mr. Guest, Yours very truly, J. HARRISON.
E. J. Guest, Esq. Kindly excuse this " curronte calamo " epistle.

Oak Mount, Helsby„ Waryington, 6th June, 1892. Jos. Harrison, Esq., J.P., My Dear Sir,— I beg to thank you for your courteous reply of the 2nd, to my letter of the Ist instant, but you must permit me to say that the words Mr. Hunt used viz :—.6 That in future he would be most particular how he summoned anyone again for a similar offence" were used by him to imply that he felt that justice had not been executed on the offending publican. In fact I know that he and his officers have been very much discouraged by the leniency shown to publicans from the bench on many occasions, and this he regarded as another instance of such leniency. Permit me to say also that jocular quotations, givtn anonymously in a court of justice, are out of place, es- pecially when they refer to a subject which requires to ,be dealt with in a spirit of the utmost seriousness. As I I think that some member of the Bench ought to make a ' public protest against the course you thought proper to I take on the occasion referred to I shall be glad tribe allowed to publish the letters passed between us. It would perhaps have been better that this should have bee done from the Bench, but as I am going from home it would be rather late in the day to do this on my return.and I fear no one else is likely to take up the matter in this way. Faithfully yours, E. J. GUEST. P.S.—I have placed this correspondence in the hands of Mr. W. Roberts, secretary of the Temperance Federa- tion, and shall be glad if you will write to him in my absence from home.

6, Woodbine Terrace. Latchford, 7th June, 1892. Dear Sir, I beg to acknowledge the receipt of yours dated the 6th inst., thanking me for my "courteous reply" to yours of the Ist inst. I regret to say, however, that so far as theremaining portim of your letter is concerned I cannot return the compliment. I may say, it is my desire to be courteous to everybody, notwithstanding which, I cannot resist the temptation to say, that your letter to me above referred to, is not only a " tree -lit " absurd, but decidedly discourteous, dictatorial, pretest- tious, and wholly uncalled for, and for these reasons you must please excuse my replying to it at greater length. Yours faithfully, J. HARRISON.

div.p: LOCAL PRIMROSE F.ErES.

WALTON.--SPEECII OF MR. R. PIERPOINT. About 300 persons attended the annual fete of the Daresbury Habitation of the Primrose League, which was held in the grounds, at Walton Hall, on Saturday. The catering was in the hands of Mr. T. 0. Speakman, of the Saracen's fled, Wilderspool. Atter the repast much mirth was caused by a Punch and Judy entertainment, while, the St. John's band, Walton, enlivened the proceedings with various selection, Mr. Thomas Lane, the bandmaster, conducting. A meeting was subse- quently held in a tent provided for the occasion— a provision that turned out to be a very necessary one, a heavy rain falling soon after the meeting opened. Lady Greenali, Ruling Councillor of the Habitation, presided. Sir Gilbert Greenall was also presqnt, but was accommodated with a chair on the floor of the tent. Amongst those present were Mr. Gilbert Greenall, the Misses Greenall, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Mr. Walter Jones (treasurer of the Habitation), Mr. C. W. Philips (hon. sec.), Mr. W. 11. J. Jenkins, Mr. London, Mr. A. Bennett, Mr. John Weir, Mr. Wm. Whitlow, &c. Lady Greenall remarked that she had taken the chair as Ruling Councillor, bat would rather have given the position up to someone else. She hoped that the rest of the evening would be pleasantly spent. Mr, T. C. London proposed "That this meeting of the Daresbury Habitation of the Primrose Le tgue congratu- lates the Marquis of Salisbury and the Government on their success at home and abroad, on the pacification of Ireland, on their most tNeful legislation, and on the years of unabated peace which the kingdom has enjoyed under their guidance." (Hear, thar.) Mr. A. Bennett seconded the motion.

Mr. R. PiEarOiNT, the C inservative candidate for Warrington, expressed his pleasure that they not only had Lady Greenall in the chair, but the pleasure of seeing their good old friend, Sir Giloert Greenall—(applause)— : who he was exceedingly glad to know was in good health, well, and strong. (Hear hear.) When people wanted substantial useful measures' such as the Con- servatives had given, they went in for a change in the constitution such as the repeal of the Act of Union, and they were ever tinkering with the constitutions of the United Kingdom. As an instance of how the Radicals acted when things were wanted he referred 'to the island of Cyprus. The island was a poor one, and the inhabitants once sent a deputation over, when the Gladstonians were in power, asking for help in education, in agriculture, and other matters. And after full consideration Lord Kimberley gave them a Constitution instead ; he gave them a Parliament of their own. They could not get help in their educational needs, but were given a Parliament, which could do nothing in the matter because of the poverty of the island. As there were two religious in the island, the Mohammedans, who were few, and the Greek Christians, who were numerous, it was decided that there should be 18 members of this House of Representatives, and it was so arranged that there were nine members of either side, the governor thus having the power. But the ' Mohammedans were so angry that they joined in with the Greeks, with-the result that 13 were on one side and six on the other. The tinkering of the Gladstonians showed that they seemed to think that the machinery would go better fcr it. It reminded him of the man whose clock went wrong and he took it to pieces. He said there was a wheel too many, and so he took it out, and then it did net go at all. (Laughter.) With regard to Ireland he referred to the feeling of the Nonconformists against Home Rule. In 1888 an address was presented to Lord Salisbury and Lord Hartington from the Nonconformist minie`ers of Ireland, signed by no less than 864 out of a total AO9O ministers, protesting against Home RulQ. No kis than 126 of those who did not sign the address were in favour of it, so that amongst the Nonsonformist ministers in Ireland there were only eight in favour of Home Rule. It seemed difficult to speak of these matters without ap- pearing to raise the religious question, but he could not help thinking that it would be a hard thing for the Pro- testants if they were ruled by a majority of Home Rulers. Let them pass Home Rule, and they would certainly have a far larger number of Irishmen come to the English labour market than at the present time. The Radicals said sometimes that the prosperous state of Ireland was owing to the be ief in what Mr. Gladstone was going to bring forward. He did not understand that argument. It weird be like trying to make the criminals of England better by abolishing the criminal laws, and establishing "Union of Hearts." They had not only to look for a party who passed laws—which might be by mistake bad ones, but they must look to a party that would carry out the laws enacted, and conduct the affairs of this mighty Empire. (Applause.) In Lord Salisbury and Mr. Bilfour they had men determined to carry out the affairs of the Eripire so as to preserve its greatness and its glorious history, and who were determined to have "peace with honour." (Applause.) Mr. John Weir supported the resolution, which was carried with cordial unanimity. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall for their kindness in allowing thP use of the grounds to the Habitation, and Lady Geenall having suitably acknow- ledged, the meeting closed.

div.head: GRAPPENFIALL.
div.p: GRAPPENFIALL.

Under the auspices,.of the Grappenhall Habitation of the Primrose League, a garden party was held at Grappenhall Heyes, on Whit-Monday afternoon, Mr. J. Charlton Parr haying kindly placed his grounds at the disposal of the members. Amongst those present during the afternoon were Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Alderman Harrison, Mr. Alfred and Mr. Frank Greenall, Mr. R. A. Naylor, Mr. Alan Lister Kaye, Mr. James Parry, Mr. J. and Mr. W. Leyland, Ac. Mr. Parr addressed a few words to a number of the visitors who had assembled in front of the house and he proposed that the officers of last year be re-elected en maw, with the addition of Mr. William Barbour, of Appleton Thorn, as warden. (Hear, hear.) Mr:Ka ye seconded the proposition, and said that at the present time the habitation had 500 associates alid 22 knights and dames, which showed an increase on the previous year of 50. The poposition was carried. The officers elected for the coming year are—Mrs.' Parr, ruling councillor; Mr. Greenall, hon. treasurer; Mr. Kaye, hon. secretary wardens, Messrs. Edward and Thomas Hanley and Mr. Wallace for Latchford, Messrs. Ashcroft, Longshaw, and Spencer for Grappenhall, and Messrs. Roughsedge, Mitch, and Barbour for Appleton. During the afternoon a cricket match was played be- tween Grappenhall and Latchford, which resulted in an easy yictory:fortheiformer,t he scores at the finish reading —Grappenhall, 63 Latchford, 30. About 450 persons Sat down to tea, the caterer being Mr. 'T. E. Speakman, of the Saracen's Head Hotel, Wilderspool. Tltp St. , Paul's Brass Band from Warrington played selections of music during the afternoon, and also for zancing in the evening. APPLETON. The annual fete in connectimi with the Appleton Habitation of the Primro-e Lfacue, was held at Apple- ton Hall, the residence of sir. T. H. Lyon, on Whit- Monday. The weather wao very fine, and there was a large attendance, probahty over 800 people being pre- inegvenwinegre. the attractions. Mr. E. Ackerley, During Sopeortosouarnned of ho Wiaan, delivered en eldress. The platform was occu- pied by Mr. T. H. Lyon, ruling councillor, Mr. T. H. Lyon, Mrs. Loge", Wright, Mr. C. Manion, Mr. S. Marson, .LP., Mr. ircnne-Jones, Mr. H. Darbyshire, Mr. C. Mactyer. Mr. 1. "Sankey, Mr. 'r. Darbyshire.—The Chairman moveethe 'adoption of a resolution express- ing confidence in Lord Salisbury's Government, and pledging the nesting to support the candidature: of Mr. Alan di Tatton Egerton.—Mr. Logan Wright Seconded th, resolution, which was adopted unanim- oustv.—Nt • flallowes expressed an opinion that Mrs. T. H. LOU ought to be presented with a badge of hon- our foram work whith she had done in connection with the Fpnitation. (Cheers.)

- DRBSCOT UNTON.—CONTRACTS FOR PROVISIONS, tr,c. Persons desirous of contracting with the Guard- ians of this Union, tor the next six months, tor supplying at the Workhouse the several articles hereinafter named, viz., Flour, Oatmeal, Margarine, Cheese, Eggs, Groceries, Coal, Linen and 'Woollen Drapery, Sruallwares Tinware. Hard- ware. Ironmongery, Earthenware, Boots and Shoes. Leather, Hay and Straw, Brushes. Collins, and other articles, are requested to deliver Sealed Tenders, upon forms to be ob- tained at my office at the Boardroom of the said Union in Whiston, on or before Thursday, the 16th June before 10 a.m. Such Tenders will be opened at the meeting of the Guardians' on the last named day. The Guardians will also take tenders for New Milk and Fresh Butter for 12 months. Samples of ' unperishahlo articles required may he seen at the Workhouse. Security will be required for the performance of the con- tracts. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender. By order of the Board, A. Y. MANN. Union Clerk,
Union Offices, Whiston, Prescot, 2nd Time, 1892.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SAT URDAY, JUNE 11. 1892.

Mr. BRUNNER, M.P., in addressing Old-age the Watermen's end Porters' Asso- Pensions. ciation, at Runcorn, on Tuesday, eendeinued various proposals for providing old- age Pensions by the aid of the State. He advised 'Members of Friendly Societies never, as long'as they lived, to accept charity at the hands of the !tltt°, but to be self-reliant, and depend upon the ''mlest results of their own work. A similar view 114 been taken at the annual meetings of the various Friendly Societies which have been held ,tinriog the week, the impression being that there great danger of the Societies losing their Ihert3' if they once permit State inter- fl * rene°. Of coarse, if anything was done by the State which weakened the healthy do- to depend upon Friendly Societies for l'revisicm against sickness and burial, it would national calamity; but it seinns to tthat there is danger of confusing the issues, idging from the turn the diieassion is taking. ; rie"lY Societies, as they are at present consti- 'llted, do not seek to provide old age pensions the, Provide for what are calle I " sick benefits" "nd 'death payments ;" and it would be an alto- "her new and ini altogether qa;ationable (leper- to tack on old-age pensions at this .Petipd of their history. It has required half eentury of experience to arrive at sound liata ill connection with sick and burial pay- ; and some Friendly Societies have in the Meantime become insolvent, through not IMderstanding the law of averages as to sickness Mort 3alit How if a system of old ago pay- +lllhenta were .broun4lit into operation ? Would t-ere not be a serious risk,for a tine, of insolvency toilb°,llg!l offering, in competition, benefits which hnt prove to be beyond the means of particular itt°dgeB) already weakened, it mar be, by being too .c-iah in the matter of payments in case of sick- to,,,e434 and death ? The larger societies, it is true, ! exercising considerable supervision over I:Pc lodges ; but what of societies where each ia practically independent!' It is amongst ben' class that insolvency exists ; 'aid there would danger of that insolvency increasing under p41:4,-w and Possibly ill-digested system of old-age ih:'lnante. State pensions wc uld have at least x.„13, advantage over every oti,er in that they Vid have the stability of the State. Qtther, in considering this great question it .1-0":1-11d be borne in mind that there is a large por- te,„ tile poorest of the poor who are not even ro-Illeers of Friendly Socio ties, and who could no than e ake provision for old age by their means that they could fly to the moon. It may be said ttlld it would just be the same with this class vot.e,r Mr. CITAXTBRRL.UN'S scheme ; and so it and it is a fatal objection to his plan. ',..11•1t • tolst use of telling an agricultural labourer ertaY £.5 down, and tl per year for 20 years? wholeles of that kind are not wrought by men Amo_ 'eve to keep themselves and their families tn'llllo twelve shillings per week. And yet they 4nd on with nothing before them in old to 8 nllt the Workhouse. What has Mr. BRUNNER tile 43' t° this class ? Is it quite sufficient to tell no+r4 t„,nrelY upon Friendly Societies ? We think sh,ol,lt 18 for such men as these that pensions `4 be provided; arid should be provided in such a a 70.118 will be no strain upon them. For our part provi`lciv.e seen nothing as yet to equal the plan of nooli,ingn pension for every member of the corn- it6Y, rich and poor alike. The rich in taking thin, ild feel that they were getting some- aliecliri return for the extra taxes they had been DoororuPoll to pay, while neither they nor their brethren would feel, when they were all

upon the same footing, that they were objects of charity. What if it did cost, say, 20 millions per annum? That is not a sum to stagger a nation which is adding to the national wealth at the rate of 150 millions every year. The people who work hard and bring up families upon less than twenty shillings per week are not getting a fair share of the results of their labour; and it would he no more than an instalment of justice if provision were made by the State for an old-age pension without calling upon them to pay a penny—except, like other citizens, in the shape of rates and taxes. Let Friendly Societies mind what they are about ; they aro doing good work; but they will make a mistake if they step out of their track, and take a burden upon themselves which should be borne by all for the benefit of all.
music THE Warrington Association of for the Amateur Bands are to be congratu-

People. latecl upon the admirable arrange- ments they have made for performances in the Park during the summer months. Already the inhabitants have had a taste of the quality of some of the bands, and, judging from the large 'attendances, they evidently like it. But the collections on the spot in support of the move- ment are, as they. always have been, a failure. Indeed it is not worth sending the hat round for the little that is received in this way. It may be that some of the ratepayers, knowing that the Corporation have made a grant of £25 per year, think they contribute in this way, and that this is the best way of contributing. But will not pay for new music for so many performers-- to say nothing of remuneration for services—and something more requires to be done. Special solicitation by authorised persons would no doubt be more successful ; but it would pro- bably mean that the burden of contributing would fall on comparatively few. It is, at any rate, worth trying; and, if it do not succeed, the Town Coun- cil must be asked to increase its grant. Music for the People in the People's Park is a form of Socialism to which, we are inclined to think, very few ratepayers would take exception. The lives of the toilers in our large towns require to be brightened and beautified, and music call be made a moans to this end as well as flowers, and pic- tures, and books. The Association is fortunate in having Mr. T. J. DowN as President, a gentle- man who has done so much for the encourage- ment and development of musical talent in War- rington. It is getting on for ten years since he formed his orchestral band ; and he has spared neither time nor money in sustaining it. The mem- bers are continuously supplied, at his expense, with the latest and best instruments and music ; and, as there are over forty members, it will be seen that this in itself is no small tax. Mr. Doww, in one way or another, cannot have spent less than £1,500 on the orchestra since it was first formed ; and there is no sign as yet of limit to his devotion and generosity. He has continued to do good in this respect by stealth ; and we should hesitate to make him blush to find it fame, if it were not that we, hope, by making these things known at this junc- ture, that other men who have means and love music may be induced to emulate in some degree the good example which he has set. Mr. F. MONKS C.C., is another gentleman who has at all times shown himself ready to assist in the movement for providing music for the people ; and, like Mr. DOWN, lie is not tired of the task. It seems to us that if this Association of Amateur Bands can be kept going, and accomplish the objects which it has in View, it will prove to be not only a constant source of delight to the inhabitants, but be the means of discovering and developing talent which may secure Warrington such credit in the world of muse as it has obtained in the world of art. Be that as it may, the town will be all the better for containing within its borders a number of well-trained bands. An admirable beginning has been made, and, with due encouragement,there is every reason to anticipate an admirable result.

div.head: MANCIIICSTRIL SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: THE MANCIIICSTRIL SHIP CANAL BILL.

The Manchester Ship Canal Bill having passed through the various stages in the House of Lords came before the Examiner of Private Bills on Thurs- day in the House of Commons,and he found that the standing orders had been complied with. SUNDAY TRAINS AT RUNCORN. The official announcement of the Sunday trains from Runcorn. which commenced last Sunday, states that the morning train leaves Chester at 9-35, calling at Ilelsby 9-47, Runcorn 9-55, and arriving at Liverpool; (Lime-st.), at 10-25. The evening train leaves Lime-st. at five o'clock. calling at Runcorn at 5-25, Helsby 5-37, and Chester 5-50. These trains will not be of much convenience to the Runcorn people. A train each way about half past one returning about 3-30 in the evening,would ' be of some ad vantage CLOSING OF RUNCORN DOCKS.

The Manchester Ship Canal Company have posted notices at Runcorn announcing that the river entrance to Runcorn Docks will be closed on and after the first of July, until further notice. Dur- ing the period the docks are closed the traffic will be conducted through the Delamere Dock at Wes- ton Point and the Weston Canal. ' Traci .irs are informed that they shall have the same facilities they possess at present for carrying on their busi- ness; To conduct the traffic as proposed.there will be considerable extra cost, and we understand that the Construction Department of the Ship Canal Company will be responsible for this. The reason for the closing of the docks is the difficulty of pro- ceeding with the river works, especially the partially demolished Bridgewater Lock, whilst the tide was allowed to hinder operations twice every twenty four hours.
WARRINGTON MEN IN COLLISION AT WINNINGTON.

An extraordinary accident occurred at Winning- ton, on Sunday afternoon, and. though no serious consequences resulted, it was little short of *a miracle that it did not prove fatal to one or more penons. MrJoseph Taylor, of Lostock Gralam,was driving in. a trap from Barnton, and when on Win- ningtoa Bridge a similar vehicle, in which two Warrington men, named Roberts and JOntioi, were riding, collided with it. Each trap was turned upon its side and rested on either side of the bridge. Th.- occupants clung to their seats, and while P.C. Richardson, of Barnton, and Mr. Adam Goodier held the horses, they were en abled to alight, When the vehicles had been disen gaged from one another, it was found that, beyond a little damage to the steps, the traps, as well as the occupants, had escaped without injury. SUDDEN DEATH OF A. CHESTER WOMAN AT NEWTON.

On the arrival of tirie—t-iliin.at Newton-le-Willows, due at 4.25,0 u Saturday afternoon,a woman named Dehlin Holliday, 54 years of age, was lifted out of a third class compartment in an apparently dying condition. She was placed upon a seat, and medical aid summoned. Dr. H. Watkins was soon in attendance, and he ordered her removal to the Legh Arms Hotel, where she died about 40 minutes afterwards, from chronic bronchitis and syncope The deceased was the wife of George Holliday, a fish and poultry salesman of 11, Broek-st., Chester. She had been on a visit to her daughter at Daub- hill, near Bolton, and on returning had to change at Kenyon Junction. On entering the Manchester train, a gentleman in the compartment named Williams noticed that she appeared very ill, and lon reaching Newton he called the attention of the station master to her condition. She was then re- moved, and the gentleman and his wife, who were et route for \Vales, accompanied her and remained with her until she died as stated. Iler relatives were communicated with, and the body was re- moved on Tuesday. She leaves 10 children, all of whom are grown. up. UMBRELLAS ItEcorEitim.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-Bt., Warringtou.—Adv:.

"A Working-man."—Your admirable letter will appear in our next issue.—We have also an ex- haustive communication from our correspondent " Manlius" which we hold over. It completely pulverises the Tory claim to have passed as many measures as the Liberals in the interests of the working classes. Mr. John Heywood, Manchester, has issued an admirable guide to the Ship Canal. It is full of information, well illustrated, and the price is one. penny only. 1
The Emperor of Germany and the Czar of Russia met, on Tuesday,and embraced each other. This may not mean much; but it is at any rate better than going to war or threatening war.
Mr. A. G. Sparrow is to be the Unionist candid- ate for Rossendale, in opposition to Mr. Maden. If he expects to succeed where Sir Thomas Brooks failed, he is certainly a very hopeful Sparrow.
Mr. Chamberlain cannot forgive Mr. Gladstona because Mr. Gladstone takes no notice of Mr.
Chamberlain. "Incredible stupidity" is the latest language used; it sounds violent and brutal; but it does not mean anything ; it is simply Joseph's way of swearing.

Why protest against long trains for ladies? It is the fashion; and a lady will do anything, any- where, at anytime—if it be the fashion. The trains are certainly extravagant, dirty, disgust- ing, and useless. No, not useless ; they can be utilised in sweeping crossings.

The General Association of Licensed Victuallers has had an interview, in private, with Mr. Coningsby Disraeli. It is stated that his views gave every satisfaction, and he will therefore receive their support. But why a private inter- view on public questions? He ought to be questioned now by the temperance party, and his answers made public.

The Tories are seeking to make political capi- tal by quoting the speeches of Mr. Gladstone before he developed into the Liberal of to-day. It is a very poor task ; but, if they will go back in these matters, why not quote the late Lord Beaconsfield's description of a Tory Goverment " as an organised hypocrisy," or his designation of Toryism as the mule of politics which engenders nothing?

The " Daily News " says :—An arithmetical question " up to date" has been sent to us by the chess editor of the "Scholastic Globe:' A gradu- ated income-tax is levied on the following principle: An income of £lOO pays a penny in the pound; one of £2OO pays twopence per pound, &c., the increase being always a penny for each hundred of income. Find the greatest possible income anyone can have after payment of the tax.

The weather of Whitsuntide has been glorious, and has made holiday folk feel; like " Tam o' Shanter," " o'er the ills o' life victorious." There were excursions here, there and everywhere ; the usual overcrowding and the usual delay in getting home; but happily not the usual serious railway accident. One excursion, on Tuesday, was from Stafford to Windermere and back for 4s. 6d. ; case of getting up soon and getting back late,with plenty of riding for the money.

It is pretty well understood that large sums of money are being subscribed by the liquor trade with a view of influencing electors where there are candidates who are favourable to them. But what of the Corupt P ractices Act? The opinion of eminent counsel has been taken, and it would seem that money spent in this way may Void an election or result in imprisonment. Beer is not King in these days ; and it is as well that the fact should be generally known.

Language is sometimes used to conceal thought as well do reveal it. Mr Chamberlain, writing to a Welsh Unionist candidate with reference to his attitude on the Howe Rule question, says that "it is utterly untrue that he was converted to the principle of Home Rule before Mr Gladstone, and that he abandoned his conversion only because his draft was rejected by the right hon. gentle- man." All this may be true ; but it is only part of the truth ; and it doesn't get rid of the fact that the member for West Birmingham declared himself in favour of the principle of Home-Rule even when he was opposing Mr. Gladstone's Bill in the House of Commons.

Councillor Dixon put a question on the niinutes of the Watch Committee, and another question of which he had given notice in due form, to the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, at the meet- ing of the Warrington Town Council, en Tuesday, and in both CMOs be was told that he was out of order. The questions were pertinent enough, and ought to have been answered. It would seem that he cannot speak without being ruled out of order. How is it? Is he always wrong? It would be as well in these cases if the Mayor would mention the Standing Order which is being violated, so that it may be seen that there is no possibility of his wor- ship himself being out of order.

It was rather hard on Mr.RobertPierpoint to ask him to speak, after the Panch and Judy perform- ance at Walton, on Saturday. The Primrose Leaguers must be amused; and Mr. Pierpoint, guilty as he is of diversions, cannot be said to be diverting. Besides, the Puneh and Judy man always has a programme, while Mr. Pierpoint hasn't found one yet, although he has been as far as Africa in search of one.

We are disposed to help the Tory candidate in his difficulty. He has promised to follow in Sir Gilbert Greenall's footsteps ; and Sir Gilbert de- clared himself, in 1885, in favour of autonomy for Ireland. That was when he was in league with the Parnellites ; and, as the Tories are again de- pending upon help from the Parnellites, why should not Mr. Pierpoint declare in favour of autonomy ?

It is noteworthy that Mr. Pierpoint reverts to 1885 in quoting the advice of an Irish member, who said they must not put trust in the promises of the Liberal party. At that time the Irish—for once—trusted the Tories ; and they soon found how shamelessly they had been betrayed in the matter of "No more coercion," and " equal laws." The Tory candidate should go one step further, and quote the advice which that Irish member gives to-day.

Mr. Pierpoint, not for the first time—said" he could tot help thinkLig it would be a hard thing for the Protestants if they were ruled by n majority of Home Rulers." He doesn't of course read his opponent's speeches, or he would know th at Dr. Houston has shown that there is really nothing to fear ; and, further, that the Catholics of Dublin have shown themselves much more tolerant in appointing Protestant officials than the Protestants of Belfast have in appoint- ing Catholic officials. Besides,it is notorious that the leaders of the Home Rule party have generally been—not Catholics but Protestants.

For the benefit of the Tory candidate and other politicians who need enlightenment on the ques- tion, we give, in another column, a letter by Dr. Houston, which appeared in the Dublin "Daily Express" of Monday last. Referring to this letter the Dublin" Evening Telegraph " of Tues- day says :

As Dr. Houston shows in his letter to the " Daily Express," the Catholics of Ireland show no trace of the miserable bigotry of a section in the North. In Dublin he gives a list of the Protestant ealploygs in the Corporation. Dublin Catholics have for next. year selected a Protestant Lord Mayor. In Cork and other places Catholic toleration is the same. In Belfast two Catholics get employment out of thousands. The creed of toleration there is that of Lord Enniskillen, who said in 1886:—" I say to you farmers—many of whom I see around me—employ more Protestants, and don't employ Roman Catho- lics. Roman Catholics must live, and they may go elsewhere to live, and joy be with them; 1 say, if you don't feed them they will have to be fed in some other country, and they will leave Fermanagh,

. . The remarks which Alderman Harrison made the other week on drunkenness have naturally excited a great deal of attention. They were so extraordinary—so much like a brief for publicans in general—that they have been strongly con- demned not only, locally, but by "The Alliance News " and the "Liverpool Porcupine." The I protest made by the Warrington Temperance Federation has been followed by some correspon dance, and by a courteous and dignified protest from a brother magistrate—Mr. E. J Guest. As will be seen from the letters which we reprint, the correspondence has had• two efilipts upon Alder- man Harrison; it has cansed him to explain that he was in a jocular mood when he made the dis- tinction between intoxication and drunkenness; and further, ceasing to be jocular, he has written what seems like an angry letter to Mr. Guest. I But perhaps this is only another phase of his peculiar merriment. lfowever, it is something gained that tlte errant justice has explained himself away. The police will know that "he didn't mean it"; and they will go about their duty in the usual way.

div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

A meeting of this Board was held on Thursday after- noon last, Mr. Mercer occupying the chair. CONTRIBUTION ORDERS.—The Clerk said he had to submit contribution orders upon the overseers for the cnrrent half year. Ells estimate was £25,187, and that was approvad by the Guardians in February last. The books had now been balanced, and he had given the overseers credit for £4,748. There were two small items unaccounted for on the rural portion of Eccleston and and:Windle, and it would leave the total of the present order at £20.040.

TIM GUARDIANS AND TIIIIIR PIOS.—The Rev. S. A. K Sylvester said there was a matter he wanted to bring before the Guardians. The matron had asked him to do what he could to relieve her of a burden and responsi- Mty which was very heavy upon her at that moment. , AS the Guardians well knew,they, in the Prescot Union, possessed a magnificent herd of pigs, and that herd of pigs had got to its present reputation entirely by the devotion and care 'winch had been bestowed upon it by the late master. At the present mcment there were applications for more than half a hundred p;gs from various parrs of the country. Perhaps the committee would have a meeting that 1 afternoon and take trtat matter into consideration, amid would then arrange to hold a conference and set the whole matter upok its right fo3ting. Ile pointed out that they received a considerable profit on their pig- keeping account. And he saw from the last half-year's account that the surplus upon pig-keeping was £32 15s. 84., and he believed he was correct in saying that in other half years it had been more.—Mr. Tyrer se- conded tile proposition, with the addition that the com- mittee consist of all the farmers on the Board.—The proposition was agreed to.
