Monday and Tuesday were observed as a general holi- day by the tradespeople of Widnes,while the large chemi- cal workr always glad of a short relaxation from his arduous toil, was granted more leisure than he de- sired, the works of the Alkali Union having stopped work for nine dare. This means a loss to the town in wages of about £7,000, a serious matter to both workmen and tradesmen alike. The reason for this long stoppage is stated to be over production. Real holiday weather has favoured the Whitsuntide holidays, and on Monday thousands left the two railway stations for Southport, Blackpool. Liverpool, and other pleasure resorts further afield, while large numbers crossed Runcorn Bridge in order to witness the processions in the Cheshire town. On Monday there was a great influx of population into Runcorn; on Tuesday, on the contrary, there was a great exodus from the town, which was exceedingly quiet. At the Railway Station 900 were booked by the Liberal Club excursion to Lianheris and other parts of North Wales, and 160 went ta Llangollen by ordiaary trains. The passengers to other places were : Liverpool. 1,100, Frodsham 850, Cheater 415. Rene Vue 274. and Northwich 255 ;making a total of 3,954. Weston Wes- leyan Sunday school organised a river trip to Liverpool, and about 800 persons were conveyed by the steamship Primrose, under the charge of Mr. Harry Hill, pilot. The annual excursion of the Mersey Missions to Seamen also took place on that day, and proved as popular as usual. about 1,000 persons taking advantagm of the sail. div.p: A WIDNNS ATEILKTR n 4 TROUBLE.

Samuel Morris a well known runeer. of Appleton, was brought before the Whines magistrates, on Thurs- day, to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly and also with assaulting P.C. Jennings while in the exe- cution of his duty.—Mr. Knowles defended. It appeared that about 11-45 on Saturday night, the 4th inst., two me* named Hughes and Jones were fighting in Victoria- road, and the constable got hold of both of them. One of the men was immediately taken from him by some bystanders, and while he was struggling with the other Morris and three or four other men set upon him. Morris seized him by the shoulders and arm and shook hie, violently, at the same time kicking him and throw- ing him on to his knees. While he was in that position, Morris punched him with his knee, and then the con- stable drew his staff to defend himself. He struck at Morris's arm, but the blow hit him on the head and Morris then ran away. The constable also struck an- other of his apailants, and went to the Polic Station where he reported the occurrence. Afterwards Morris was apprehended at Dr. 0 Keeffe's aurgery where he had had a wound on his head" • dressed. P.S. Ma Cracker said Morris was very drunk, and in the doctor's surgery he was very violent and refused to pay the doctor's fee.—P.S. MeGregor also stated that Morris was very drunk.—Mr. Knowles said he had not come there to say that Jennings, was a vile perjurer but he was mistaken. He would call floe witnesses who would state Morris never interfered with the constable at all, or laid hands upon him, when the officer took the two fighters into custody. A strange man interfered with him and then ran behind Morris and his friend. The officer struck at him, with his stsff but instead of hitting the arm, it fell upin Morris's head. Morris Was in drink, but it was denied, that he was drunk.—Albert Hornby, John Quinn, Frei Jones, Michael Hughes, and Thomas McGurl all stated that it was a " strange man" that interfered with the Con- stable and that Morris, took no part whatever.—The Bench imposed a fine, of 103. and costs for drunkenness, but said there was a doubt in regard to the assault, and they would give the prisoner the benefit of it.—Jones, and Hughes, were charged, with committing a breach, if the peace, and were each hound over for three months. ! PRESCOT GUARDIANS AND THEIR, WORK.

The report of the work and expenditure of the Prescot Board of Guardians during the half-year ended 25th March last has just been issued by the Clerk (Mr. A. F. Mann). The total expenditure, after deducting receipts, including contributions from the county council (£3,958), St. Helens Corporation (£2,636), farm accounts, ire., amounted to £18,528 15s. 9d. The school atter:dame committee expended an additional sum of £142 19i. 7d!, making a grand total of £18,669 15s. 4d. The items of expenditure included— Maintenance of poor in workhouse, £3,447 4s. ; maintenance of poor in hospitals or schools, £1,359 . 10s. loa. ; relief to outdoor poor (including non-resident), £6,712 4s. 7d. ; and cost of tuna- tics in asylums, £2,852 133. 4d. A total of 8,119 persons had been relieved during the half-year against 7,845 in the corresponding period last year ; and 2,396 vagrants and tramps had been lodged and relieved against 2,570 last year. On the Ist January last there were 848 persons in the workhouse in receipt of relief, against 618 last year ; and 3,024 outdoor, including lunatics, paupers in hospital, &c., against 3,750 in the previous year. The average cost per head per week for inmates in the workhouse had been—provisions 2s. against 2s. 4d. last year: necessaries is. against is. last year ; and clothing 7/d., against 6d. last year. The following figures show the number of persons relieved from the various townships of the Union—Hold 15, Cronton 6, Ditton 99, Eccleston 1,533, Hale 10, Hale- wood 24, fluyton-with-Roby 80, Knowsley 19, Parr 708, Prescot 388, Rainford 85, Rainhill 45, Spoke 0, Sutton 435, fatback 12, Whiston 2,389, Widnes 2,717, Windle 1,109, Little Wootton 22, Much Woolton 298, lunatics in asylums 284, paupers in hospitals or schools 258, nost-resident poer 1, total 10,515.

div.head: WIDNES COAL DEALER AND HIS WEIGHING MACHINE.
div.p: A WIDNES COAL DEALER AND HIS WEIGHING MACHINE.

At Widnes Police Court on Thursday George Davies, coal dealer, of Kalerdale Terrace, Al bert-road, was summoned for having had in his possession for use in trade a weigh-bridge which was incorrect.— Inspector Kilpatrick said he visited the defendants' ,coal yard in Elizabeth-street on the 26th May, and he examined a four ton weigh-bridge which was used for weighing loads of coal as it was sent out to customers. He found the bridge was 2.81b5. out of balance to begin with, and when weighed up to the extent of a ton it was 701bs. out of balance against the ' purchasers. By the weight book lie found that five loads of coal had been weighed on the machine that day, and the defendant would benefit to the extent of 3 cwt and 14 lbs. If the machine were in that state for a week he would be the gainer by 18 cyst and 3 quarters.—By Mr. F. J. l'oole (who defended) : There were no signs of rough usAge about the machine, it appeared to be out of order through ordinary wear and tear.—Mr. Poole said Mr. Davies had this machine adjusted by Messrs. Noisy some months ago and he was told that it would be all right for twelve months and he was not aware that they were wrong. Ile had a large business and he was compelled to leave these details to his servants, but his orders were very strict that the machines must be kept in good condition.-9 fine of 40s. and costs 12s. was imposed.—Maria Moores, grocer, Legh-at., was summoned for having a pair of unjust scales.—The Inspector said the scales were 37 drachms against the purchaser. The scales were hidden beneath the countet, and the defendant denied that they were on the premises. Afterwards she said she did not use them.—The defendant reiterated thus statement, and , said she had only a little toffy to sell. As the woman was very poor the Inspector did not press the case, and a fine of Is. and cots,l4s. was imposed. The scales,beiug , worthless, were forfeited.

div.head: WHITSUNTIDE FESTIVITIES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: WHITSUNTIDE FESTIVITIES AT RUNCORN.

Glorious sunlight, and a refreshing breeze favoured the Whitsuntide festival of Runcorn, which was celebrated on Monday last, and the in- flux of visitors into the town was in consequence larger than for many years past. People arrived in large numbers from Northwich and Winsford by boat, and by train from Sr. Helens and Warrington, &c., and about two thousand crossed Runcorn Bridge. This was not the "big year" as it is locally known, that is, the friendly societies were not mak- ing their most gorgeous display, but a new and in- Wresting feature was provided in the shape of a

div.head: TRADES PROCESSION.
div.p: TRADES PROCESSION.

The Upper Mersey Waterman sand Porters' Association had been the chief organisers of this demonstration which was characterised by an event as unusual as it was interesting. Devonshire Square was the place of assembly, and at half-past nine there would be abtout four thousand people gathered there to witness Mrs. Brunner, the wife of our respected member, Mr. J. T. Btunner, M.P., unfurl to the breeze a new banner which had cost the Mersey watermen 53 guineas. The lady gracefully performed her allotted task, and those present then saw a beautiful banner, having a representation on one side of the Bottom Locks Warehouses, and on the other a river steamboat, otherwise a Duke's Packet, drawing a line of flats, and also a canal steamer. After this ceremony Mr. Brunner delivered an appropriate address, which is reported in another column, and then the procession started. The Upper Mersey Watermen's and Porters' Association led the way, to the music of Mill Brow Brass Band, and then came members of the following trades societies t—Shipwrighte, bricklayers, coopers, bakers, joiners, boilermakers, and cloggers. There were about 500 in the ranks and the procession was grestly admired. The members wore their regalia and carried banners and baunerettes, besides emblems of their respective trades. After parading the principal th)roughfares,they returned to the Union Hall in Regent- st.' the headquarters of the Watermen's Association, and there dispersed. It is hoped this procession will become an annual event.

div.head: TIM DUKE'S CLUB
div.p: TIM DUKE'S CLUB

which is now over 100 years old, marched through the streets to the music of Oossage's Band. Captain Johnson and Mr. Hoeworth walked in front as marshal's and then came the band and banner. Immediately behind the latter walked Messrs. John Meadowcroft, F. Wiswall, J. K. Digges, J. Done, and T. Simister and Dr. Mangan and Dr. Robinson, the rear being brought up by 60 menalvers. After the usual parade through the town the members went to the Parish Church, where a brief service was held, and the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood delivered a sermon on temperance. The brass band accompanied the singing in admirable style. The other friendly societies that demonstrated were the Loyal William IV. of Oddfellows and the Duke of Edinburgh Lodge of Ocidfellows, who followed the usual course of marching to Dalton. In the afternoon the PROCESSION OF SCHOLARS
took place, and the streets were lined with spectators I In fact they were 411 but implssab,e, In former years

big enunca SCUOOLS have acted independently of each other, but, acting on rt hint from the vicar a united procession ?nil held on the present occasion. The scholars assembled at the National Schoois,whence they proceeded in the following order through the town and on to the Vicarage at Higher Runcorn Parish Church 500 scholars, Holy Trinity 224, Ragged Schoch 140, St. Michael's 30, and Mersey Mis- sion 268; total 1,43 g. Goesage Dandled the Parish Church and the Mill Brow File and Drum Band (organised by Miss Evelyn Preston) headed goly Trinity School. Ban- ners and streamers of every device and hue were carried, and the demonstration was Imposing and plea- sant to look at. Tea was provided for the children at their several schools, and entertainments were held in the evening.

div.head: NONCONFORMIST SCHOOLS
div.p: THE NONCONFORMIST SCHOOLS

united as usual, the order of procession being deter- mined by the date of the establishment of each school. The chillren A•sembled at their respective schools, and took their positions in the procession as it wended its way along. The order and numbers in the procession were as follow :

Brunswick (Wesleyan) St. John's (Presbyterian) 296 St. Luke's(Congregational) 167 Bethesda (Congregational) St. Edwards (Catholic) Primitive Methodist 296 Mill Brow (Wesleyan) Methodist Free Church 219 Camden (Wesleyan) Nelson-st. (Wesleyan) 3190

Whilst several of the schools marched to the inusic of brass bands, others were accompanied by their chapel.' choirs singing hymms, and the effect was highly plea- sant. The school banners and bannerettes were carried and their bright colours glistened in the brilliant sun- shine. Each school was accompanied by the minister, and , ..ef officials. In the ranks of the Camden scholars, hea .og the boys, was a beautiful new banner, the gift of air. Philip Speakman, C.C., who is superintendent of the school. On the front was emblazoned the title of the school and the date of its establishment, and on the reverse aide was the Biblical injunction set out" Watch and Pray." The procession went through the chief thoroughfares, to a field in Ilalton.road, kindly lent by Mr. Williamson. After spending a short time here, the children returned to their respective schoole, where they were treated to buns, &c., and various entertain- ments were held in the evening.

ItXCHAIIII7.9. The members of the Union Tent, No. 215, made a new departure by taking pt in the Whitsuntide display. They walked in procession through the principal thoroughfares, starting from the Cocoa Rooms in High. St. Leading was the Westen Point Salt Works Band, then came the banner of the Tent, followed by Bro. Rev. J. Pulford Williams, Bros. R. Evans, D.C.R., J. Lead. Stone, P D.C.R. J. E. Warburton, D.S.,and J. Lea,D.T. The symbolical' regalia of the Order was carried as follows : Sword, John Hayes, guardian ; Sun, 11. Caw- ley. C.R. ; Moon and Stars, J. Booth, D.R. ; Beehive, H. Page, P.C.R. ; Cross Keys, W. Franklin, treasurer; Inkstand and pens, J. Clark, acting secretary ; Tent, W. E. Hough, assistant secretary; Dove, E. Boden, Levete ; Lamb, W. Matthews, trustee ; Jewelled Crown, W. Egerton, trustee ; Wheat Sheaf, F. Clarke, trustee ; Bible. J. Sayle, chaplain ; Serpent, J. Coat, sick steward ; Eye. J. Millington, book steward. In the ranks were 100 adults and 60 juveniles, and, adorned with white scarves, they looked extremely well, and the demonstration is considered the best the Tent have had. Bro. R. Smith, of the Manchester Past Officers' Encamp- ment, was present, and wore the splendid Encampment , regalia. A number of members of the Charity Tent also took pert. Tlia procession made a stoppage at Mrs. Lea's T.mperance flute, where the band played a selec- i tion of musk. CAMP' MERTINGS. The Primitive Methodists held their customary camp meetings on Runcorn Bill, on Sunday. At half-past ten the congregation worshipping in Greenway-road IChapel, assembled in Devonshire Square and marched in processional order to the Hill, singing as they pro- , Iceeded. In the early morn there had been a heavy downpour Of rain, and the threatening aspect of the , weather prevented many from taking part in the meet- ing, and the attendance was very meagre. Earnest ad- dresses were delivered by the Rev. C. Finch, Mr. W. C. 1 Hill and Mr. C. Lewis. In the afternoon the congreg a- bon after parading a number of streets again held a meeting on the Hill, and about 3,000 persons listened to the addresses delivered by the Rev. C. Finch, ReT. H.
Davenport, and MesrP. W. Jones and R. Peacock. In the evening a Love Feast was held in the Chapel.

Although the town was so throng.d, the best of order prevailed throughout the day, and Supt. Atherton (who had made every arrangement) and his men were not called upon'to take any severe measure. There was also apparently less drunkenness than usual, and only two men were taken into custody tor being drunk and disorderly.

div.head: F ItODSHAIf ,
div.p: F ItODSHAIf ,

TEB WHITSIINTIDI FESTIVITIES—The proceedings OR Whit-Monday were on somewhat similar lines to those which have prevailed fer many years past. As usual, Main-street was filled with the usual paraphernalia attendant upon festivities, and the proprietors of the various concerns did a very remunerative business. The principal items in the programme, however, con- sisted of the procession of Friendly Societies, namely, the Foresters, Druids, and Oudfellows. They met at their lodge-rooms about nine o'clock, formed into pro- cessional order, and marched to the Parish Church, where a special sermon was preached by the Vicar, the Rev. H. B. Blogg. Each society was preceded by a band —the Foresters:by Helsbv, the oddlellows by Frodsham Old, and the Druids by the Church Band. After leaving the sacred edifice, they proceeded to the Vicarage, and afterwards visited the residences of a number of the principal inhabitants, and then repaired to Castle Park, the grounds of which were thrown open, through the kindness of the Misses Wright. Here some time was enjoyably spent. Then the members returned to the respective hostelries where their lodges are held. They partook of substantial dinners,admirably served by their respective hosts, Messers. Youd, Ecimumlson, and Fletch- er. The post-prandial proceedings were of a highly enjoyable character. It is gratifying to be able to re,ord the fact that although a large number of visitors were in the town, there was an entire absence of rowdyism, and very few persons indeed were to be seen the worse for drink.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WA RRINGTO N.

A week or two ago I mentioned that Mr. Hemp- son, the Conservative agent, had, in a letter to a newspaper, complained that, during a ten years residence in Warrington, he had only been visited by two Church of Englund clergymen. I admitted that Mr. Hampton would know best what he was most in need of, and that, being a Conservative agent, he was a likely person to benefit by the visitations of the clergy. In conclusion, as I felt interested in this groping after spiritual light from an unexpected quarter, I expressed a hope that Mr Hampson would let us know if his complaint had had the deoired eff-tct.

I have now to acknowledge Mr. llampson's courtesy in forwatding that information in a letter through you, Mr. Editor. It is rather discourag- ing to find that, notwithstanding his very public complaint he has " not recently been visited by any clergyman, preacher or missionary." But Mr. Hampson is not vindictive. Although the clergy have not looked after him as he thinks they should have done, he declines to have anything to do with disendowment or even disestablishment. In fact he is disposed to excuse them by saying that it is a " well-known fact "that he has recently " become so good" that he is now almost as " good a Pharisee " as anybody need want to see. --I . . _

This is satisfactory to some extent, but still, I must confess, not quite so satisfactory as it might have been. It is a pity that, when Mr. Hampsoix did take the trouble to" become good," his good- ness took the direction of Pharisaism, but—every one to his taste. Besides, one mustn't expect too much for a beginning. I feel certain that the coming election will provide ample cause for Mr. Hampson to cogitate upon' the vicissitudes and dis- appointment of life,and it is just possible that he may in the end get a stage or two higher than Phar- isaism.

Poor Councillor Dixon gets called most merci- lessly to order in the Warrington Town Council. When he rises, the words, You are out of order" seem to come as automatically out of the Mayor's lips as though it was a formula that had a neces- sary connection with Councillor Dixon standing on his feet. I must say, that, although Councillor Dixon often draws upon himself the Mayoral peremptoriness, I cannot think he is by any means exceptiotal in the Council in being out of order, yet it does strike me that while Councillor Dixon is almost incessantly being corrected from the civic chair, other members of the Corpora- tion are sometimes allowed a licence.

Now, I do not any that Councillor Dixon's de- mand for some expression of opinion upon Alder- man Harrison's recent charge to the police concern- ing the publicans was strictly in order, but I think ho had quite as much right to raise that question as Alderman Burgess had to raise that of Councillor Dixon's motives for depreciating Dr. Norman Tate's report on the Lofigial ;.',;p3t zlni;tion for doing which the Aldeiman received no check from the Mayor at all. I must confess that Councillor Dixon's question was quite as much in order in the Council Chamber as Alderman Harrison's remarks which gate rie to it were on the Belle), They amount practically,if he is going to act consistently with them, to a proclamation of plenary indulgence to the publicans so far as bej, Concerned.

Idl ma Last week I gaid Moon why the local Roman Catholics and Noncouforrithts—and Jews for that 'matter—should not vote in the ConserVative direc- tion. Now I will give the Warrington shop assist.. ants one for casting their vote on the Liberal side, and it will be opportune so soon after the time when there has been so much agitation in favour of the halt holiday, already secured, and earlier closing. It ought to be remembered that it was by a Liberal Government that the Shop Hours Regulation Act. of 1886 was passed. This Bill provides that no person under the age of eighteen years shall be employed in or about shops for a longer time than 74 hours, including meal-Limes, in any one week, and makes other stipulations for the better, protec- tion of the class concerned. Those whom the Bill immediately concerns will not possess the franchise, but their older and electorally qualified brethren in the trade ought to consider this matter in deciding on how to record their vote in the coming election.

,1 Some time ago the Chief Constable of Warrington on an application being made for sanction for an extensien of the Lion Hotel, objected that the alteration would involve the construction of an entrance in Ship Yard, which would be the means of increasing drunkenness. The question of the dangers of these back entrances to public-houses which was descanted upon pretty pointedly in the "Examiner" at the time, has, I see, been brought up at last week's meeting of the Toxteth Guardians, Mr. Jones submitted there a motion in favour of petitioning the city justices to limit the number of back entrances to public houses, which was carried with but one dissentient. Warrington Guardians and Town Council also please follow this example when the occasion presents itself.

Whit Monday in Newton was not distinguishaMe from any other Monday in the year, except perhaps that tie village was a trifle quieter. The attractions for visitors and picnic parties are fast ebbing away, and the beautiful sheet of water, called " the lake,' will soon be a thing of the past, so far as the general public are concerned. At one time, and not very long ago either, there were as many as eight or nine pleasure boats plying on the lake, and it was • common sight to see them packed with people on holiday occasions, enjoying the beauties of its sur- roundings. Now all this is changed, and two solit- ary hulks are to be seen at times plodding along over the surtace of the water, with perhaps a single or it may be two occupants in each.

_— A wealthy resident has had a magnificent boat house erected on the side of the lake,and furnished it with a boat for his own especial use, and it can, of course, only be assumed that the common fry will not in time be allowed to enjoy the same privileges, as the gentleman named. But why P ; Perhaps at the General Election speaking tour, Mr. I Legh will have an opportunity of explaining why the only attraction for visitors Newton possessesis being gradually withdrawn from their use. But this is not all ; the road to Castle Hill has also been blocked, and visitors, and even residents are not allowed to avail themselves of the pleasure of a ratable to this famed spot, so dear to the hearts of young people. This, also, is another question which requires an explanation.
MERLIN.

At St. Helens, on Friday, James Turnbull, attendant at Rainhill County Lunatic Asylum, was tned 40s. for assaulting an imbecile patient -named Peter Cassidy, by kicking him in the back. Defendant said be had been attacked by Cassidy, and did it in sets-defence, being afraid of other patients attacking bitn a Cassidy over- powered him. He had only cloth boots on. Forty shillings is the minimum penalty, the maximum being £2O.

CHARGE OF ASSAULT ON A YOUNG WOMAN. I • James Marsh, an unmarried man, "ous stove fitter, of o , Wellington-St., was charged at the Warrington 3, • Borough Police Court, on Tuesday with assaulting, the ' • previous night, Mary Lawrenson, a young woman em- • ployed by Mr. Mayhall, tripe seller, Buttermarket-st. (I'' The charge was at first, one of indecent assault, but was altered to that of aggravated assault. The prisoner and another man named James Berry rushed into the shop at five minutes past 11 at night, when the door was closed, and asked for two pennyworths of chip potatoes, and afterwards committed the assault—lie denied the charge, but was fined £lO or in default two months' imprisonment. —The prisoner paid the fine. CHARGE AGAINST BOYS OF DAMAGING CORN.-1 STRANGE DEFENCE. Percy Davies, 29 Croft-st., and Walter Avory, 54 Oliver-st, boys, were charged with doing damage to growing oats, the property of Peter Norcott, to the amount of 15s.—P.C. Cooper, 20, proved the case. Davies said a man met him in Crosslev-St. and threatened ...;" to shoot him with a pistol he had if he did not co with • him and get him sons grass out of the field.—Alderman .1, Harrison (the Chairman) : You ought to have had more sense than to be frightened by a threat of that kind.— Inspector Cox said the man mentioned would be charged on Monday with firing the pistol on the highway, with carrying it without a license, and with cruelty to a pony. —The lads were fined ss. and costs each. HORRIBLE CHARGE AGAINST A WARRINGTON TRANESMAN. At the borough magistrates court on Tuesday, John Richard Massey, widower, a hairdresser, and umbrella maker, at 77 Winwick-st., was charged with criminally assaulting Malin half-past eleven o'clock on Sunday night, his daughter, Edith Massey, aged 12 years. Dr. Starkey Smith, gave evidence that criminal assaults had frequently been committed on the girl, and testimony was given by Ellen Griffiths and John Devon, as to observation of prisoner's proceedings made from the street through his bedroom window, which was low and had no blind. The prisoner, who emphatically denied the charge, was remanded for a week, the megistrates agreeing to accept bail for his reappearance. Inspector Uphill, agent for the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, was in court, and the magistrates • conferred with him as to sending the child to the work- house for the present, and with the prisoner's consent, II(' she was sent thither, 5h3 having been formerly there.— The prisoner found the bail, himself in £5O, and two E.O surieties in £25 each.

Collier, in Buttermarket-st., the same night, 10i. and 6s. 6d. costes.—Martin Hart, in Bridge-st., on Satur- day, 9s. 6d. including costs.—Elizabetb Ellison in Carlisle •11, et., on Saturday night, 10s. and costs.—John Mullaney nod in Friar's-green, the same night, 9s. 6d. including costs. *A —Julia Ann Shields was charged with being drunk and disorderly and refusing to quit the Old Crow Inn hal kept by Mr. Roberts. He said he always refused to serve her as she persisted in making disturbances, and he did so on this occasion. She was drunk and made a disturbance as usual. She was sent to prison for a month with hard labour. WIFE ASSACLT.—WiIIiam Riley, marine store dealer, Buckley-st., was brought up in custody charged with ' assaulting his wife Rebecca the previous night. The Chief Constable said the prisoner, left home on Friday .siln • morning for the purpose of collecting rags and Ift bones, and returned about an hour earlier than customary in the evening. His half brother, a soldier named Dagnall, was over on furlough, and while he was out had procured some drink and • weet te the complainant's house, and with her and • her mother consumed it. When the prisoner came in • he found his mother-in-law drunk in bed, his wife ly- ing on the same bed, and his brother lying in a bed in another room. The complainant stated that when her sins , husband found her in bed, he picked up a boot and in- ' dieted with it a severe wound on the back of her head 'PI' and also a more serious one on her hand, which had to 041* be dressed at the Infirmary.—The complainant corrobo- 11% rated this statement.—The prisoner said his wife was mu drunk every day, then went home and had a sleep, and in he dare not trust her with halfpenny, and had to do everything himself. She had cut his head open many a time. He had never been up at that court before.— The Magistrates' Clerk : You have been here once for w, not sending your child to school,and once for assaulting your wife.—The prisoner: I wish you could separate ' us.—Wm. Smith deposed that the prisoner's wife took • , the poker up to him and he knocked it back and it struck her, causing the wound on her head. Witness did not know how her hand got injured.—The prisoner: She hit me first with the poker first thing, and I shoved it away, and it hit her.—The prisoner was bound over ,-se- to keep the peace for six months in his own recogni- lin Bailees of £.lO, and two sureties of £5 each. BREACH or :rue Ganz Laws.---Peter Rowson was tr. charged with being found by a constable at Bank Quay, • , on the night of the 28th of May, in possession of a net and stakes with which it was suspected he was going to Catch game.—The defendant : I was going to catch rabbits. I told him so.—The police officer deposed to seeing a dng coming from Litton Mill way at Bank Quay t on the night in question, and the defendant came behind it with another man. The latter had a bag and as soon as he saw witness ran away. Be overtook the defend- ant, and asked him if he had anything in his pockets, but he said nothing, and would not allow him to pull his coat open to see. He found a net and eleven pegs .113 iii his pocket, and he said he used them for VII rabbit catching. He gave the name and address— James Holden, 17, Factory Lane, but witness and In. r.. spector Spinks found there as no such number there. , , —The Constable: He told me he would give me a vise Couple of rabbits if I would let him off—the defendant denied having had any game on him, and exclaimed : "Do you think if I had game I would be a fellow like tnat take it from me. It is enough to make his heart !Limp out of his inside when you look at him:, (Laughter.) The defendant was tined £1 and 78. costs, in default 14 days' imprisonment, the net and pegs to be forfeited. FIGHTING.—John Hardman and Joseph Hanlon, for fighting in Blackhurst-st., the previous night, were bound over to keep the peace for 6 months, and had to pay 7s. costs each. Carrington, in Bank Park, on the sth inst., 14s. 61. including costs. - As IMMORAL COUELE.—Catherine Ellison was charged with being guilty of vagrancy and immoral behaviour, in Mill-lane, on 'Saturday night, and Peter White, of N.. 6, Dial Court, was charged with aiding and abetting. Ellison was fined 55., and White 53. and costs, the alter- native being seven days imprisonment in each case.

I TUESDAY.—BePore Mr. R. Garnett (chairman), and Alderman Harrison. AN INSUBORDINATE PAUPER.—Annie McGuire was charged by Mr. B. Shearer, with being disorderly and insubordinate in the workhouse, on the previous day. Mr. Shearer said the misconduct consisted of refusing to enter the receiving room and going into her bedroom. She took off all her clothes and said she would be taken in that condition if she went.—The evidence was that the prisoner behaved in the manner described, on coming in at night after the proper time for coining in, and on being requested to go into the ward. On Mr. Duckworth endeavouring to "ether into the receiving room she got hold of the tender to strike him with.—The prisoner who pleaded not guilty, was sent to jail for seven days with hard labour. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Patrick Kilroy was charged with being drunk and disorderly and doing damage to the window of one Kilroy, in Friars' Green, the previous afternoon, to the amount of 2s. 6d. A police con- stable gave evidence as to the first charge, and the prisoner who pleaded guilty in both, was fined 101. and costs.—William Edelsten, drunk and disorderly in Edelsten's Yard, on Monday night, ss. and costs.— James West, in Ship Yard, the same night, ss. Dirt:NlL—John Connolly, in Bridge-street, the previous afternoon, was fined 2s. 6d. ASSAULTING THE POLICE.—Annie West and Michael Maher, her father, were charged with assaulting P.C.'s Leathwood and Roper in Ship Yard on Monday night. P.C. Leathwood said the prisoners were fighting, and he got the assistance of P.C.Roper to take them into custody. West came behind them with a belt, and struck witness several times on the back and also Roper on the head, and caused it to bleed very freely. Witness took the belt from her, and Maher, while he was struggling with her, struck him several times in the mouth. Roper was ' obliged to leave the woman to come to his assistance. The woman said if her brother had been there no one would have taken them into custody.—P.C. Roper cor- roborated, and a woman said she saw Leathwood hit by West, who struck her several times in the mouth, and kicked her in the stomach.—Both prisoners were sent to jail foe two months, with hard labour. AN Aunty DESERTER.—James Hindle, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in St. James's- St., on Monday night, and with being a deserter from the Scotch Greys. He was sent to Strangeways Jail, for the latter offence, m await an escort, the first charge not being dealt with. , Scaoot CASES—SEAM Fags: EnacaTioN. —The follow- ing persons were dealt with, on the prosecution of Mr. G. Riley, for not sending their children to school :—Mary Bennett, 120, Pierpoint-st , who exclaimed :—They call it free education, but I have paid 10d. school money since the last time I was here.—ln reply to Mr. Garnett she said she paid for the education of her son who was in the third standard and attended Heathside School, the sum of 2d. a week.—The Chairman said education was practically free, and he could not accept without better authority what she said about paving 2d. a week for a child in the 3rd Standard.—Mr. Riley : Yes, Sir, it is so in this school.—The Chairman : It is a little unusual. —Hie defendant : I have another child in no standard at all that pays id. per week.—The Chairman : A penny a week won't do you any harm.—The defendant: No, Sir, I don't grumble at it. She was fined 55., and on leaving the court remarked, "There is no justice in Warrington."—Henry Forster, 80, Lythgoe's-lane, Peter Garland, forgeman, Watkin-st., 2s. 6d. ; Mary Garrity, rag gatherer,sent to St.Anne'slndustrial School; J.Grirne, labourer, Glasshouse-row, ss. ; Benjamin Matthewman, brush maker, 3, Scott-st., 2s. 6d. ; Thomas Moody, forgeman, 36, Pierpoint-st., Richard Ridgway, joiner, 67, Ellesmere-at., Walter Lovatt, boiler maker, 37, For- sha.w-st., ss. each. ; Patrick Wade, forgeman, Gee-st., Win. Tryner, forgeman, 48, Pierpoint-st., ss. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mt. John Fairclough and Alderman Wright. Delmar AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Miller was chargad with being drunk and disorderly in Rose and Crown- street, the previous night. A constable said the defend- ant's wife complained that he had locked her out in the street and threatened to murder her. On witness going up to the defendant in the street he found him drunk and he used disgraceful language to him on his com- plaining to him. He was therefore obliged to lock him up.—lie was fined ss. and Costs. THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley (chairman), and Couwillor James Fairclough. ASSAULT ON A Woutor.—George Boardman,forgeman, of Stamford-st., was charged with assaulting Sarah Woodall, of the same street on the 4th of June. He was bound over in the sum of £lO to keep the peace for six months.

THEFT OF BOOT3.—Mark Burke, was charged with stealing about nine o'clock on the morning of the 19th of March last, a pair of boots from the shop door of Frederick Jenkins, 94 Bridge-st., and was fined 103. and costs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Catherine Smith and GPO. Marsh, in Rose Yard, the previous night, were fined 83. 6d. each, including costs.—Mary Connolly in Rose Yard, that morning, and in Scotland-road, in March last, sent
FRlDAY.—Before Aldermen. Harrison (chairman) and

Wright. AN ABSENTEE MILITIAMAN. —James Tatley, labourer, was charged with absenting himself from the training of the 3rd South Lancashire Militia, and was fined 403. and costs ; in default 14 days' imprisonment. CHARGE OF THEFT . —John Warburton, labourer, 323, Winwick-road, and Richard Lowe, labourer, 43, Tilley- st., were charged with being found in posession of a paviour's mallet, supposed to have been stolen.—D S. Monaghan deposed to seeing Warburton with the mallet in Mersey-street, the previous afternoon, and his leaving it on the footpath when he saw him. He said ha bought it of Lowe. Witness found Lowe standing at the corner of Academy-st . and Buttermarket-st., who stated that it belonged to him and he had sold it to Warburton. They now re- peated their statements, and Lowe said his father had been a pavior and the mallet had been his.—They were remanded till to-day. DRUNK AND DISORDRRLY.—James Towey,in Winwick- st., the previous night, who had been using bad langu- ageagainst some people holding a religious meeting, ss. and costs.

_ A NIGHT SLEEPER IN THE Ph.RlE.—Mary O'Reilly was charged with sleeping in Bank Park the previous night without havinz any visible means of subsistence, and doing damage to the shrubs to the amount of 10s. She had been lying among the shrubs. She was sent to prissn for 14 days hard labour. NON-MAINTENANCE OF Bus BOY—Thomas Taylor was charged by Inspector James with non-contribution for the maintenance of his son on board the "Clio," and was ordered to pay is. a week. ASSAULT.—James Frangleton, of 8 Gandy's Terrace, was charged with assaulting Martha Dagnall, 9 Gandy's Walk, on the 6th inst. She did not appear, and the case was dismissed. QUARRELLINE WOMEN.—Mary Shaw, 26, Glazebrook- st., and Charlotte Owen, of 46 in the same street, were charged with threatening each other in Glazehrook-st., on the 7th inst. Owen was bound over in £5 and had to pay the costs ; and Shaw was dismissed.

BENEFIT OF THE BOUHT.—William Fallon, Nelson-st., was charged with resisting P.S. Strickland and P.C. Cochrane, whilst they were arresting defendant's brother on Saturday night.—The officers stated that whilst they were struggling with Thomas Fallon the defendant came up and endeavoured to take him from them—Defendant said he was taking his brother home at the time, and denied that he resisted the officers.—Defendant was given the benefit of the doubt, and the case was dis- missed.

KICKING A CONSTABLE—George Barrett, Caroline-st. was charged with being drunz and disorderly and with assaulting P.C. Jennings.—The officer stated that he was taking the prisoner to the Police Station on Saturday night, when he became very violent and kicked him on the side.—Fined 2s. 6d. rpd costs for the drunkenness and ss. and costs for the assault.

DISORDERLY CONDUCT ON RUNCORN BRIDOE.—Mary Ann Parker and Matilda Holland, young women, were charged with disorderly conduct on Runcorn Bridge at midnight.—Parker, an old offender, was sentenced to a month's hard labour and Holland was sent to gaol for seven days. DRUNKENNESS.—John Roberts, Peter Purcell, Mary Carney, Catherine Owens, William Platt, Sarah Jervis, Christopher Daley, William Egan, Margaret Ferney, Joseph Brundell, Elizabeth liushell,:Edward Davies, and Annie Farmer were each fined for drunkenness. BREACHES OF THE Pilacii.—The following were charged with committing breaches of the peace and were bound over in the usual sureties :—Michael Mannion, Annie Pool, Mary Whalley, Catherine Harrison, and Mary A. Hyland. James Traynor was summoned for using threats to Thomas Film and he wits bound over.

ODUFELLOWS. Speaking at the resumed conference of Oddfellows, at Derby, on Thursday, Sir William Harcourt said that he attended as a visitor so see how that great association conducted its business, He was gratified to find that the society's work afforded a striking example of the general self-government of which Britain had so many proud instances.

NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL. The annual meeting of the Notts Incorporated Football Club has been held, but only shareholders were addmitted and the balance sheet has been withheld from the public. It is estimated that the club is £1,700 or £lBOO in debt. It will be remembered that they commenced the season £BOO or £9OO to the bad. Their gate receipts are said to be £BOO less than in the previous season, and players' wages are reportcd to have cost £4OO more. As against this there has been a reduction in the expenses of training and in other directions. Bad as is this statn of things the shareholders are facing it with a good heart, and they have great hopes that the debt, or, at any rate, the bulk of it, will be cleared off by the bazaar they are promoting. The Duke of Portland has been elected president of the club, no doubt in the hope that the duchess will lend eclat to the occasion by performing the opening ceremony at the bazaar.
Mr. Harry " Yu;

Furniss had better remain inside of the offices of " Punch " rather than trust himself at a prizP fight or a football match ; or at any rate, if he does allow himself a little recreation of this clia-acter he ought never to express an opinion. For Mr. Furniss to say that a pugilistic encounter was a drawing-room enter- tainment as compared to a professional football match is such utter '• rot" as to lead one to suppose that Mr. Furniss has never seen a professional football match, or has been drawing very much on his imagination, perhaps not a very unusual occupation.

--- Blackburn Rovers F.C. have had a very bad season. The balance sheet has just been issued, and their total liabilities are £l.lBl 45., but against this they have their splendioly fitted ground, so that they are not in a state of bankruptcy by any means, and considering that they have expended over £2,200 on what may be termed capitel acclamt during the past two years, their position is not bad. Their wage list is very moderate—£l,s62 03. 6d.—and, in fact, all the expenses have been kept down.

-- It is, says the" Athletic News, " curious how the York- shire Football Committee and players and clubs in the Wakefield district get at loggerheads. Herbert Folios is the latest victim to the committee's iron-covered fist as they have suspended him because he declines to ask the Corporation to which ho is Town Clerk to postpone its business while he interviews the more important authority at Leeds. Illustrating one's authority is all very well in its way, but the average outsider will think that these constant attempts to bring individuals to their knees savour too much of the autoratic to do any real good, ,or to cause the said authoriey to be held in reverence and respect.

CRICKET. The oldest cricketer living is Mr. C. Absolon, a hale and hearty veteran of 75 years of age, who has been as- sociated with cricket in the South of England for 61 years. He is a native of Wallingford, in Berkshire, and played his first match when 14 years of age at Cowley Marsh, near Oxford. Over 40 years ago he became a re- sident in the London district, and there are very few grounds in or near London on which he has not played.

He has never been a first-class player, according to the general acceptation of the term ; but in club matches, for the last twenty years he has averaged close on 1,000 runs and about 200 wickets. Be is still a very smart fieldsman in almost any position, but his usual place when not bowling "slows" is at short slip. This year he has so far played in five out of the 60 matches on his list (in all of which he trusts to take part), and though he is rather disappointed with his batting, he has taken 38 wickets.

He completed his 75th year last Monday, and no one would dream that he is within 20 years of his age. His step is as firm and elastic, and his eve as keen and bright, as these of scores of men who haven't half his weight of years to carry. .

Berkeley, the Oxfcrd slow bowler, is not naturally left-handed. When a boy he strained his right arm badly, and his doctor forbade him to use it for bowling. Practice with the left hand soon surmounted the diffi- culty, and taught bim to use his left equally well.
WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY . AUTHORITY.

A meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, yest3rday iweek. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present, Messrs. Long, A. Jolley, Dignam, W. Houghton, Kilshaw, Fairclough, Owen, S. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (surveyor), F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector), Dr. Sephton (medical officer.) BURTMWOOD DRAINAGE.—At a meeting of the Im- provemeau and Lighting Committee it was decided that the Surveyor should now complete this drainage scheme in accordance with the wish of the Local Government Board, and report to the Committee with an approxim- ate estimate of all costs at a meeting to be called pre- vious to the July meeting of the Authority.—The report was adopted. PLANS—rho Surveyor recommended that the plan of 24 houses in Liverpool-road, Warrington, for Mr. John Lloyd be passed.---adopted.

, THE PROPOSED' MAW BURIAL GROUND' AT Rix- TON .—A letter was read from the Local Govern- ment Board stating that they had now under consideration the. report of their inspector who held the inquiry at Rixton was right to the proposal to borrow £1,700 for the purpose of providing a new burial place at Rixton. They pointed oKt that there was no proposal to erecta; chapel on the consecrated part of the ground, while the Act of Parliament did not seem to contemplate any exemption from this.— The Clark said that if they erected a place for the Church of England theother denominationsmight require chapels alse,and .as the whole of the ground was only an acre in extent there would be little left if they put three or four build- ings upon it, II part from the erepense their erection would entail on the township.—lt was decided, after some-con- versation, that the Clerk should write to the Local Government Board fully explaining the circumstances of the case, and pointing out that what was wanted was really only an extension of the present burial ground.. TIGH SMALL-PDX OurnaoAxs—The Clerk reported with regard to the recent outbreak of small-pox outside , the borough boundary in Latchford. He said he was I informed of the cases about two o-clock on the after- noon of Sunday, the 15th May, .and after communicat- ing with Dr. Fox, the deputy medical officer for the borough, Alderman Burgess, the chairman of the Sani. tary Committee, and the Town Clerk, all the infected persons were removed to the infectious diseases hospitql by seven o'clock the same evening. He mentioned that Dr. Willett who had been in attendance in those cases, . had, on the 10th, sent a notification,, but owing to a misapprehension he had sent it to the Rural Sanitary Authority instead of Dr. Sephton, and hence arose the delay in securing isolation. A letter was read from the Town Clerk, of Warrington on behalf of the Sanitary Committee, urging the Authority to adopt the Infectious Disease (Notification) Act, and the Infectious Disease (Prevention) Act, and after a short discussion the Chair- man gave notice that he would move at the next meet- ing that these Acts be adopted.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS DEATHS OF SPELTER WORKERS.
div.p: MYSTERIOUS DEATHS OF SPELTER WORKERS.

On Tuesday morning an inquest was opened by Mr. Jones,.deputy coroner, at the Warrington Work- house, concerning the deaths of John Connor aged about 37. years, and William Henry 'Yates, aged 28, labourers at the spelter works of Messrs. Kenyon, Bank Quay. Mr. Richard Johnson, assistant factory inspector, was present, and Mr. Arthur Browne represented Messrs. Kenyon.—Mr. Browne said Messrs. Kenyon, wished him to say that they were deeply grieved at the death of these two men. They could not imagine the cause, as they had carried on the works for 20 years and had never had an accident which resulted in death. They, therefore, courted every inquiry by that jury.—The Deputy Coroner explained that the deceased had been working at the spelter works in thel 'r previous week and were taken ill. They were immediately attended by separate doctors, Con- , nor by Dr. Braide, and Yates by Dr. Adams, who had certified that Connor died from peritonitis, and Yates from acute jaundice. Both doctors at the time said that the certificates were consistent with the causes of death, but from circumstances that came to their knowledge that both were taken ill, and that a third man was similarly affected, they came to the opinion that it might be a very different reason—metallic poison- ing, arsenic poisoning, or fumes from a furnace.—Mrs. Martha Yates deposed : The deceased was her hus- band, and lived at 4, Back Aiken-street, and was 28 years of age. On Monday last, May 30th, he started working at the spelter works, that being the first time he had worked there. He was in good health, but when he returned on Tuesday evening at five o'clock he cam- plained of feeling very ill in his stomach. He was sick, . and Dr. Brooks Caine and gave him some medicine. He said that he had got some sulphur on his stomach. Dr. Adams saw him on Wednesday at breakfast and attended him to the time of his, death, but he died on Thursday morning at twenty-minutes to five. She knew nothing of the arrangements at the works.— Mr. Browne said there was no sulphur at the works whatever.—Patrick Donohue, of 9, Bostock-st., said Connor had lodged with him. He started working at Messrs. Kenyon's works on Monday ef the preceding• week, all right in health, but on Tuesday at tea time came home ill, and next morning he said some of the " stuff " had got down his throat. One of the men had told him (deceased) that he ought to have a handker- chief over his mouth. Dr. Braide was brought on the Tuesday night and gave Connor some medicine, and he again visited hire on the following morning, the deceased afterwards being removed about 12 o'clock on the Friday to the Workhouse Hospital, where he died about two hours later. Nurse Daniel deposed to. deceased's admission to the Workhouse Hospital, and death in less than two hours after.— Mrs. Mary Donohue corroborated the statement that Connor said he had some " stuff " down his throat. He said he was working at the barrels and was told to put a handkerchief round his mouth, and that if be did not the stuff would injure him.—Joseph Hardman, 18, James-at., stated that he started work at Messrs. Kenyon's on the last Thursday in May, and worked a day and a half. He laboured in the yard the first day, wheeling bricks until three o'clock, when he commenced wheeling spelter. He felt no worse for it the first day. He worked with the barrels from six next morning, and about noon he began to feel ill all over. He was dry and sick, and he gave up about 2.30 in the afternoon. He tried to work again, but his feelings left him, and he hardly knew how he got home, though he remembered falling in Bold-st. The foreman, named Spencer, en- gaged him, but gave him no instructions that there was any danger. He did not know whether the , firm provided cloths for the men's mouths, and he heard no one complain whilst he was there.— Mr. Browne said that the firm did not provide cloths.— A juryman : Were any experiments going on 2—Mr. Browne : No.—Hardman further stated that the stuff was damped. He had been in bed until Sunday last.— John Arthur Spencer, of 65 Aiken-st.,and William Higgs, Refuge Square, Bewsey, stated that they had worked as labourers at the works eight years and nine months respectively, and neither had ever felt any ill effects of the work.—Mr. David Tinnion, one of the partners of the works, said he had been in Warrington 14, years, and had manufactured this same stuff during that time and had never had any experience of an accident, although about 1,000 tons had been turned out annually. The flux skitnmings came from the top of the galvanizing pots at White Cross, and other galvanizing places in Wallington and all over the country, and con- tained about 50 per cent, of chloride of zinc, with ammonia and a little carbon,. in the form of a double salt of ammonia and zinc. This was put in a large rolling mortar mill, and ground, so as to wash out the soluble salts. They had never apprehended danger from it, as they had never had any cases of this kind during their experience. The Aux was damped as a matter of commercial interest and not as a provision against endangering the men. There was no dust in the mill in question, and neither were there any fumes in the whole works. Some time ago, Dr. Ballard was over at the works and congratulated them on the absence of the fumes. The men at the spelter furnaces wore handker- chiefs over their mouths.—Dr. Adams gave particulars of the post mortem examination of the deceased, which were consistent with the certificates previously granted. The men had acute bile, and the witness Hardman was suffering from the same complaint. He had understood that there were fumes, but he, however, thought that the illness might have been caused from the dust arisingfrom the flux .—Dr. Braide agreed with Dr. Adams's particulars of the pose mortem, but differed from him as to the cause of the complaint with regard to Connor. The latter had told him that he felt hot on the Tuesday and took a very large amount of water, which, in his opinion, was quite enough to set up the acute jaundice.—Mr. Johnson said the ease would be considered by the Factory Depart- ment, and if they discovered any danger regulations would be made. Efe, had seen the works, but from the evidence he had the opinion that there was an element of danger which needed investigation.—The Deputy Coroner said it struck him as singular that three men should be taken so suddenly ill, and, from the medical evidence, from the same cause. Perhaps it was simply a strange coincidence.—The jury considered the matter in private for a few minutes, and decided to adjourn the inquest so as to have the attendance of the foreman of the works,tne contents of the stomachs of the deceased analysed, and the works visited during operations.— The inquest was adjourned until the 21st inst.

div.head: FAILURE OF A LONDON BANK.
div.p: THE FAILURE OF A LONDON BANK.

The chief topic of conversation in commercial circles in London, is th failure of the New Oriental Bank. It is reported that efforts will be made to reorganize the bank. A" Tunes "second edition, Singapore, Thursday says the failure of the New Oriental Bank is taken very calmly here, the credit of the bank having been doubted for some time.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOLUNTEEB IN CAMP.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOLUNTEEB IN CAMP.

This year the Warrington Volunteers have joined in the encampment on Conway Marsh of the Lan- cashire and Cheshire ratfantry Volanteer Brigade. The men left Warrington at half-past eight on Saturday night, this late hour for their departure having to be fixed cng to the fact that the rail- way company, in consequence of the stress of traffic, were unable to take the Volunteers through Chester till the evening. The men assembled at the volunteer Hall at half-past seven, and, having been placed in marching order, Colonel Greenall, who was in command, addressed the men. He wished, he said,. to see the men get in and out of the train in a soldier-like, steady and orderly manner, and he alse. hoped the conduct of the Battalion at Coeway would be a pattern to other Battalions. He asked them ta, recollect that one man had the unmaking of the good name of the Battalion, but he hosed that at the end of the training he should receive on their behalf ihrom Gen- eral Thackweht his approval and congratulations at the way that Battalion had performed its part in the en- campment. The Corps then marched to Bank Quay Station, their departure being witnessed by a large num- ber of people. They arrived at their camp at Conway about 11 o'clock. Other regiments aame in very much later than that from Warrington, and the sth Cheshire only arrived on Sunday morning, having determined to travel on Sunday rather than face tAe prospect of com- ing into camp in the small hours of the morning. Thanks ta the provision made by the fatigue party :which left Warrington on the previous Tuesday and Wednesday, the Volunteers on their arrival on Satur- day night were soon comfortably settled for the night. The fatigue party, which was under Captain Baynes, had hada rather lively time of it. On the Wednesday a strong gale sprang up that they had to cease their labours. In fact, they had to undo a large amount of what had been done, the wind blowing with such vio- lence that the tents already erected had to be lowered in order to prevent their being blown away. Some of the tents were actually almost torn to ribbons- by the wind. On Thursday the gale moderated, and on Saturday morning the tents needed for the accommoda- tion of the regiment were all ready. Besides these mar- quees were put up for the officers' mess, .the sergeants' mess,store tents, ke. The arrangements for the water sup- ply of the camp—a most important point—have been un- der the charge of Mr Farrington,C.E., borough surveyor of Canway„ who has had one and two-inch mains laid all round the camp, so that a copious supply of pure water is available for all purposes. The Brigade consists of the Ist (Bury),2nd (Rochdale), and aid (Salford), V.B. Lancashire Fusiliers, and 4th (Stockport) and sth (Congleton) V.B. Cheshire Regi- ment, and the Ist V.B. South Lancashire Regiment (Warrington). The other battalion in the brigade, the 2nd NMI, South Lancashire Begirnent (St. Helens), is under canvas at Blackpool. The Warrington Volunteers are about 300. strong. The 4th Cheshire, under Colonel Ferneley, are about 900 strong, and come from Stock- port,. Hyde, Stalybridg,e, and Glossop ; the an Cheshire. under Colonel Shackerlev, are also about 900 strong, and come from Congleton, Macclesfield, Wilmslow, and other parts of Cheshire; the Ist Volunteer Battalion Lancashire Fusiliers, about 600 strong, are under the command of Celonel Yonge ; and the Rochdale Velma teers, about 500 strong, are under the command of Colonel Philli pi. The brigadier is Major General Thack- well, Cll. ; Colonel Jecelyn acts as brigade major ; Major Beidge,of the Ist V.8.5.L.R., is the brigade supply and transport officer ; and Captain Buckton, also of the Ist V.8.5.L.R., is acting as aide-de-camp. The brigade was on Thursday inspected by Major- General Sir Julian H. Hall, C. 8., comtnand:ng the north-western districts. The weather was very sultry, and busbies were wisely discarded. There was a parade of above 4,000 of ranks of the brigade. The staff officers were Major-General Thackwell, in command ; Lieutenant-Colonel R. J. 0. Jocelyn, brigade major; Captain and Hon. MAjor J. Bridge, let South Lanca- shire, supply and transport officer; and Captain Bridge, South Lancashire, A.D.C. Theparade was called for half- past ten,hur it was close upon noon before Majer-General Sir Julian. Hall, attended by Major Hall, Ist Lancashire Fusiliers, rode upon the review ground. Having acknowledged the salute, the inspecting officer made a close examination of the respective battalions. The brigade was then marched past in open and close column and in quarter column battalions. _ The, march past throughout was generally good, but there should have been better attention paid to distances, and there was a tendency, usually observable on this ground, to hang back on the .eft. The way in which several of the companies—notably certain belonging to the Cheshire Regiments—went past the saluting base, 'evoked from Major-General Sir Julian Hall, the commendatory ex- pression, ‘. Very good indeed." The brigade was.then put through some minor movements, the inspection closing with an attack on the camp, which was defended by the 4th Cheshire. The brigade having been formed into close column, was briefly ad- dressed by Major-General Sir Julian Hall, who ex- pressed pleasure aE again visiting the camp, and in find- ing that the brigade this year included battalions which had not been brigaded before. It was, in the opinion of all soldiers, most necessary that regiments of volun- teers should come together as muah as possible and meet in brigade camp, as it promoted their efficiency and instilled into them what was very needful—a knowledge of camp life and duties. As to the details of the parade, he could say he was very much pleased with what he had seen. The men, although they did not wear their full head-dress, for a cause which must be very obvious, looked well and smart, their accoutre- ments were clean and well put on. Without specifying any regiment, lie might say he had noticed some men who were in the habit of looking on the ground when on the march instead of holding up their heads and showing they were proud of the force to which they had the honour tc belong. There was also some difficulty noticeable as to the distances, but that was a question which rested inure with the markers than the men. On the whole the parade was good, although there seemed to be too many men for the ground at the dis- posal of the brigade. He was glad to learn that their conduct in and out of camp had been go,ad, which was a very satisfactory thing. The regiments were then marched back to their lines and dismissed for dinner.

Despite the great heat, there was only one occasion for ambulance service being called in—a man from one of the Cheshire regiments dropping down in the ranks just before the inspecting officer reached his battalion. The camp arrangements were subsequently inspected by Major-General.Sir Julian Uall. The camp breaks up to-day, and prior to striking tents Colonel Baker, C. 8., commanding the 20th regimental district, will inspect the Salford battalion.

TREAT TO POOR CitILDREN AT RUN- CORN. Brilliant sunshine and an invigorating breeze yesterday week favoured the treat to the poorest children of thu town of Runcorn, organised by the Committee of the Aged Persons' Treat. It would be impossible to imagine a more suitable pUrpose to which to devote the balance the Committee had in hand, and those who were privileged to witness the young people enjoy themselves to the top of their bent, registered a resolution that" a day in 1 the country " should be an annual event. 513 ' children and about 40 adults joined the excursion at one o'clock, and on arriving at Frodsham they walked in procession to Mersey View, led by the 1 Mersey Mission Fife Band. Amongst those present were a number of ministers of religion, and Messrs. H. J. Grice. (chairman of the Board of Commission- ers), S. Taylor, W. M. Soweriey, W. Hankinson,A. It. Frith, &c. A large variety of games had been arranged for the youngsters,. who were also per- mitted to have donkey rides, and to use the swings &c., free of charge. A four o'clock tea was provided, and the large staff of helpers hail a busy half hour supplying the wants of the little army. Afterwards more frolicsome fun and a Punch and Judy show, manipulated by Mr. Richard Catterall, of Liverpool. proved highly amusing. In the course of the afternoon the workers sat down to tea,at the invitation of Mr. Grice i, who was after- wards cordially thanked for the nterest he had taken in the day's proceedings. The party returned to Runcorn by special train at seven o'clock, all well pleased with the success of the outing, Each boy and girl was handed a bun and orange on leav- ing Mersey View?. The catering of Mrs. Parker gave every satisfaction.

FOUR PEOPLE KILLED BY LIGHTNING. MADRID, TRIIRSDAY.—A terrible hailstorm, causing great destruction to crops, broke over the town and i district of Linares, n the province of Jaen. Two women and two children living in a cottage in the open field near the town were, killed by lightning. It is presumed they were hsstening to take refuge from the storm, as their bodies, which were dreadfully burned, were found close to the cvttNle,, which was completely carbonised.

THE DEATH OF ONE OF THE "LIGHT
BRIGADE."

Sir,—Thomas Rodgers, aged 72, until recently an in- mate of Withington Union, died on Sunday last at 5 a.m. He was one of the few whom you and others of our local Press have tried to push their cause. Whit- week caused the mournful cortoge to be few (five). No plaintive strain of that march in "Saul" was accorded to the hero. He has now faced that last enemy, grim death. His only living, destitute coomrade in our city joined the very few friends who paid a last tribute.
His earthly struggles now have ceased ; Best, rest, brave warrior, rest in peace. My last duty to that soldier has ended.—Yours, &c., L. FLOOD. Crosby °Hotel, Withy Grove, Manchester, June 8.

div.head: "A HOLE I'TH' BALLET."
div.p: "A HOLE I'TH' BALLET."

Dear Mester Editur.—Aw'm noan up to time this wick, an' its not my faut noather. Yo' see, this holiday time is made greyt use on by church foak ; and eavvr owd church bell ez been peylin' every mornin' just ez aw wanted to get agate vvi' my rhymin'. Aw tell yo what, if eawr parsons (we'n two on urn 1) lived hauf-a-mile nearer to th' seaund o' that bell, aw'm thinkin' we shod hare a deyd seet less on it. It wudn't matter so witch if ther wur any use er sense in it; but mooastly it only rings to remind us that some saint deed theausands o' years sin'l as if that wur sufficient to justify a darn'd nuisance. And ez if it wur moor important to carry eawt a crazy fad,to savin' a poor sowl woze yed met be splittin' wi a fever fro' want o' sleep an' rest, an' wo happent to be cossed by livin' anywheer near th' church! When aw think o' wot some par- sons do, aw'm reminded very forcibly o' wot Bobbie Burns wrote:

"Mans inhumanity to man Makes countless thousands mourn." If ther wuz anay use or common sense i' peylin church bells abeawt aw wudn't say a blessed word, but ez at present advised aw caunt see it. Well, yo mun tak th' will fer th' deed, ez th' mon sed wen he axt his mate to hey a drink, an' then walk'd off beawt payin' fer it !—Yores allus, TUM 0' PEGS. Nyowton God bless o'. June 6th, 1892.

div.head: CHURCH AND RADICALISM.
div.p: THE CHURCH AND RADICALISM.

- quite fall in with your correspondent's remarks n last week's issue on the posit ion of the Established Church and politics. A Churchman and a Tory. have been too long, and with some reason, viewed as synonymous. Fifty years ago such a curiosity as a Radical parson could not be found; but now there are not only a few clergymen imbued with Radicalism, but an Archdeacon, or two, and perhaps a Bishop. If our church is resolved and wishes to retain her present ecclesiastical status this must go on. A little interest thrown by the church on the people's side, and OR the labour question—such as that shown by the Bishop of of Durham—will do more to defeat the aims of the Liberationists than all the church's support of Tory candidates can ever hope to do. A National Church should not lend its influence entirely te one political party or class. The Church's opportunities for doing good are greater than those of any other religious body in the

THE TORY CANDIDATE CANVASSING. Sir,—Many curious incidents occur during an election canvass. You alluded to one lately, viz., the shadow- ing of Dr. Houston, whilst so occupied. This was un- doubtedly an (H)ill deed, on the part of the Tories ; but I would ask permission, through your columns, to mention another. Mr. Robert Pierpoint, in the course of his soliciting travels, recently visited Whitecross Ward, and, his knock, at the door of a certain boils*, was answered by the elector in person. After the usual salutations, the would-he Tory member asked the favour of the vote and interest of his hearer, who was a bond-fide working-malt, and as puch, wanted to know what he was to receive in return. Although he pressed the ques- tion, there was no response, for the Tory candidate had no programme. The voter wanted an enquiry into min- ing royalties, with a view to their abolition ; he wanted paid labour members of Parliament, and other mea- sures for the benefit of the working-classes ; none of which Mr. Pierpoint will support, and finding that he had nothing to receive in exchange for his vote, he advised the Tory candidate to go home, as the electors required a man like his opponent Dr. Houston, who bad something to offer, in exchange for what he was asking. Rumour says that Mr. Pierpoint left the street in ques- tion, and has not yet returned to finish canvassing it. It would be a good thing, sir, for every elector to ask for an equivalent, to his vote, and not to throw it away, by voting " Blue," simply because his father did. It is somewhat strange, that the Tory candidate should be such a complete failure. He has failed as a Warring- ton man, to do anything to benefit the town of his birth, he has failed as a political candidate, being unable to offer any programme for our approval, and I venture to predict he will fail at the poll.—Yours &c., WARRINGTONIAN.

This communication was made by the Ainalga mated ,ciety, and as the pub- lic were not acquainted with its numerical strength, I thought it might be inferred,that the society represented the thoughts and views of the majority of local railway ment.on the labour question, or as 11. Ogden puts it,
THE BOHEMIAN MINING DISASTER.

It has now been officially ascertained that the number of miners who descended the Birkenbury mine, near Przibram. in Bohemia, on the 31st ult., was 507, of whom 475 ascended or were afterwards rescued alive. Thus 332 loit their lives. Up to Wednesday morning 304 bodies had been recovered. The deceased men leave 252 widows, and 692 orphans under 14 years of age.
