div.p: TITE EX \MINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 11, 18r.

" Thc interests of railway men." As a non-society man, I felt it was my duty to let your readers know the strength of the society, because I do not concede to its , claim to represent the interests, both of non-society men and its own member's. The claim is a presumptuous one, and one which many non-society men stoutly re- pudiate ; because some of the questions submitted to the local candidates are unfavourable to the interests of a large section of railway men. This is notably so in the first question, which provides for a " maximum + working day of ten hours." A boy fresh from school, and with only a few months' experience of railway work in certain sections, could tell us that this was im- possible, and yet we have men like H. Ogden,with many years' experience of railway work, advocating this ques- tion. It is also a great injustice to a certain class of men, especially locomotive men who aredependent for their work on special trains. If a man thus placed, cannot make more than ten hours in one day. he will not be able on many occasions to earn a week's wage ; because the day following he may only work from five to six hours. That a man situated like this, should be restricted to ten hours in one day is both unjust and unfair. . . _

In questions two and three, I can see nothing but that which is fair,both to the companies and their employes. But No. 4, which recommends the compulsory provision of self-acting coupling appliances, would, as 'Mr. Robert Pierpoint has already shown, be a great injustice to the shouters, since it is only a logical conclusion, which even the Amalgamated Society must admit, that the companies would no longer employ a number of men whose services could be dispensed with. Question No. 5, which provides that "certificates of competency " be granted to all engine drivers, I oppose because it suggests incompetency on the part of a body of men who have hitherto discharged their duties in such a manner as to show that " certificates of competency" are not required. The latter part of the question, which suggests that these certificates be granted by the Board of Trade, impugns the integrity of railway companies in general. With regard to question 8 and 7. which respectively provide, that contracting out of the Employers' Liabi- lity Act be made illegal ; and that members of Parlia- ment be paid. The former I oppose. oecause so far as I can ascertain, the present arrangement (especially the one on the London and North-Western Railway) between the companies and their employes, is equitable and fair. The latter is a party question, and ought not to be in- cluded in a series of questions of this character. H. Ogden's parting word to me is," That unless I can back out my inference by more solid arguments, to hold my peace." My parting words both to him and his society are, to be less presumptuous, and more logical ; when this is so, I may have occasion to hold my peace. I can see nothing in the letter of Mr. Knowles worth replying to. Apologizing for trespassing so far on your valuable space, I am, yours sincerely, Padgate. June 9, 1892.
JOSEPH DAIKIN.
"AS TO THE DRINK TRAFFIC."
Wine lea mocker. strong drink is caging; and whose ever is deceived thereby is not wise. Pro. 20.1 v. - -

Sir,—" Tory Enquirer," in the Tory local herald of drink from which lam prevented (as shown in my last letter published by you in your issue of the 28th ult.), anything like making ta brief report of an opeu air Temperance meeting, or a defence of the oppressed working-men of the town demands from me answers to the five following questions as to the drink traffic :- 1. " Has its effect on himself been such, that he has been obliged to abstain for fear of over indulgence ? 2. Can he give the number of people in Warrington who have escaped the effects of drink through total abstinence ? 3. The number of the above who were hopeless drunkards previous to signing the pledge? 4. The number of people who are able to drink moderately and do not consider that it injures them in any way." If the answer to question 5 gives a larger number than those of 3 and 4 together, can he give any good reason why those respectable persons, principally working-men should be forbidden by law and coerced into giving up that which they and 99 doctors out of every 100 con- sider good for them ? Now, Sir, your readers will easily see that "Tory En- quirer " utterly fails to show the least sign of regret, at the terrible effects of strong drink upon either myself or anyone else. He cunningly glories in its dire results, and serpent-like seeks to beguile working-men into the snares of drinking habits, the cause of " woe," " sorrow," " contentions,"" babblings," " wounds without causes' except the drink, which " at the last biteth like a ser- pent, and stingeth like an adder." " Tory Enquirer" has no sympathy for anyone thus suffering under the awful effects of drink. But as Messinger fitly brands such wolfish characters— 'The eye that will not weep another's sorrow. Should beast no gentler brightness than the glare That reddens in the eyeball of the wolf." And such mean wretches have too long ruled our unfortunate town and country. Do not we need a chi for the better? Then work and vote for it you who are not so politically heartless as "Tory Enquirer." Ile inhumanly gluts his narrow soul with the false supposition that I have so ruined my powers of body and mind that I have "been obliged to abstain for fear of over-indulgence." Suck is not the fact in my case, God in his infinite mercy gave me to see before I was ten years of age the danger of beginning to take the cursed drink. Therefore I signed the pledge which He has enabled me to keep hitherto. Would you, "Enquirer." condemn any person for acting as I have been enabled by God's help to act? If not, why don't you act likewise? And you, dear reader, also? If you have not signed the pledge on such grounds then sign! And help to amend the present sad state of our town, and country. Help us to make the world better than we found it ? " Enquirer " asks about the "number of people in Warrington who have escaped the effects of drink through total abstinence ?" I cannot tell the number. But I deeply deplore the small number, and live, and labour, as well as pray that the number may speedily and greatly be increased. Why don't you do likewise? " Enquirer " asks as to "the number of the above who were hopeless drunkards previous to signing I the pledge ?" None; for if any had been hopeless sticy roujcl rp). !3,vm had pithsr caution, endea- rent, Or will reform. A 5 Milidli says, " wtaire no hope is left, is left ne fear." But if hope be lost, then drink, drink makers, drink sellers, and drink a Ivoeates, of such a type as "Tory Enquirer "are responsible for such "hopeless drunk- ards" to men and God. Who can disprove this? And if any one eould do so. how much better and more God- like to do as we do ? Do all you can to prevent hopeless drinkers becoming drunkards. Send no man to Parlia- ment who does not solemnly pledge tkimself to vote that the power may be taken out of tea hands of such as have hitherto made the laws so as totiring the country into its present demoralised and deunken state, and watch with a keener eye and guard with a firmer hand those who administer the laws on the Bench. " Tory Enquirer" asks for" the number of people who are able to drink moderately and do not consider that it injures them in any way." This class are more numerous than the number of hopeless drunkards and the number of drunkards who are not so far gone in drink and all its attendant woes. "Tory Enquirer" asks me if I" can give any good reason why these re- spectable persons, principally working-men, should be forbidden by law and coerced into giving up that which they and ninety-nine doctors (?) out of every hundred consider good for them." "Tory Enquirer" doubtless would be the last kind of person to go from house to house to carefully ascertain about such matters and persons seeing he dreads the direct veto—the votes et all the people—on the" drink traffic." Why do he, and the Tory party oppose the" direct veto ;" the very thing which alone would give the majority the right to move in matters of this kind? Can" Tory Enquirer " give any good reason why the majority ought not to decide the number of drink-shops to be, or not to be, placed in the midst of them ? Is it not Tories in this town, in the whole couutrv, as well as in Parliament, who oppose the adoption of the prin- ciple of the majority ruling ? Therefore are not Tories the worst enemies of the rights of the people ? As to those who consider that moderate drinking does them no harm, and therefore drink they do, he says medical advisers, ninety-nine out of every hundred consider drinking good for the people. What an unblushing libel ! Is Sir William Gull, F.R.S., physician to her Majesty, one among the ninety-nine? He says—" I should say from my experience that alcohol is the Most destructive agent that we are aware of in this country. I would like to say that a very large number of people in society are dying day by day, by alcohol, but not supposed to be poisoned by it." Sir Andrew Clark, M. D F.R.C.S., of London, physician in ordinary to the Queen, says "I looked at the hospital wards to-day,and saw that seven out of ten owed their diseases to alcohol." Sir Henry Thompson, F.R.S., Surgeon Extraordinary to His Majesty the King of the Belgians, and Surgeon to the University College hospital, says :—" I have no hesitation in attributing a very large proportion of seine of the most painful maladies which came under my notice, as well as those which every medical man has to treat, to the ordinary and daily use of fermented drink taiten in the quantity which is conventionally deemed moderate." I might easily multiply such rea- sons why so-called moderate drinkers, should drink less and think more before inculcating, as "Tory Enquirer " blindly and falsely does, the merit of consuming fire- water, which ruins the bodies of some 60,000, of our fellow-brothers and sisters, every year.—Yours truly, B. STOREY.

ULSTERMEN & NATIONA.LISTS. . A CONTRAST. DR. HOUSTON MARES OUT HIS CASE. The following letter from Dr. Houston appeared in" Dublin Express " of Monday,in continuation of the controversy which has been excited by the speech delivered in Warrington. TO THE EDITOR OF THE DAILY EXPRESS. Sin,—ln my answer to the letter of your correspon- dent, "Truth," I said that if I had made any mistake in imputing to the Corporation of Belfast and Derry that they employed none hut Protestant officials, I should be the first to acknowledge my error. I, therefore, hasten to redeem my promise, so far as Belfast is concerned. I have now before me a document which, when speak- ing in Warrington, I had not seen, and of the existence of which I was then unaware—namely, the minutes of the evidence giveri on the 9th of May last before the Select Committee on the Belfast Corporation (Lunatic Aeylums, Icc.,) Bill, the Members present being Mr. Arthur Elliot, Sir Edward Harland, Mr. Hinkes, Mr. Knox, Mr. Shaw Lefevre, Mr. T. W. Russell, and Mr. Sexton. The first witness Mr. Charles M'Lorinan, a Roman Catholic ratepayer and burgess, who carries on business in Belfast, and has lived there for 60 years, handing in a memorandum, setting forth the pro- portions in which Roman Catholics are employed by the various public bodies in Belfast, a city which contains 70.000 Roman Catholics out of a total popula- tion of, I think, 273,000. If the figures in this memo- randum-are trustworthy, the matter stands thus—The Corpc.ration consists of 40 members, all Protestants, and employs 91 officials, at an annual expense of £16,610. Those are of various grades, commencing with a fortunate Town Clerk, wno receives £2,300 a year, increasing annually by £lOO, till the handsome figure of £2,500 a year is reached. This latter sum is just £lOO a year more than twice the salary of the Town Clerk of Dublin. Of these 91 officials two are Roman Catholics, viz., one of the four Superintendents of Fire Brigade and street inspectors, who among them get £720, and, as 1 infer, therefore, £lBO a year eaeti ; and the Library superintendent, who gets £240 a year. These two ' gentlemen, therefore get between them £420 a year, not one-fifth of the salary of the Town Clerk, and little more than one thirty-ninth of the aggregate salaries received by their 89 Protestant colleagues. This, it will, I think, be admitted is not very striking evidence of "Orange liberality," but still it is something to be thankful for when it is compared with that of the Harbour Board, which consists of 22 Commissioners, all Protestants, and employs 37 officials, among whom not one Roman Catho- lic is to be found. The Water Commissioners, 16 in number, include one Roman Catholic, but not one of their seven employes belongs to that proscribed creed. The poor-law guardians consist of 22 elected, all Protestants, and 22 ex-officio, of whom one only is a Roman Catholic. They have 94 employes, of whom 3, viz., 2 of the 5 workhouse teachers and 1 of the 41 nurses are Roman Catholics. Lastly, the board of governors of the asylum, numbering 22, includes 3 Roman Catholics, and employs 73 persons of whom 8 out of the 68 attendants are Roman Catholics. I may add that the petty sessions clerks, 6 in number, are all Protestants, so are the recorder, the clerks of the peace for the county and the borough, the coroner, and the sub-sheriff. Sir, the lesson to be learned from these figures is plain. The Roman Catholics of Belfast ale officially ostracised. I commend the fact to the gentlemen who are to take part in the approaching convention. 1 shall be curious to see how they will deal with it. Floods of eloquence and torrents of rhetoric will not sweep it away. lam not going to assert that some, aye, many, who will per- form on that remarkable stage will not be genuinely appre- hensive that a Home Rule government means oppression and persecution of Protestants by Roman Catholics. I dare say a number of them would be honestly ready to take their oath on a copy of Fox's Book of Martyrs that the Lord Chief Justice, the Lord Chief Baron, Lord Justice Barry,Mr. Justice O'Brien,Mr. It. P. Carton, Q.C, Mr. Wm. Kenny, Q.C. and Mr. Albert Quill—not to speak of such blood-thirsty bigots as Mr. Justin M'Carthy M.P. and Mr. Redmond, M.P.—are longing to bathe in the gore of the Protestants of Ireland, and looking forward with pleasurable anticipation to the time when fires will be burning merrily in Smithfield, and an auto-da-fe will be going on in which perhaps I shall be playing a part more prominent than agreeable. I recognise the force and persistency of prejudice, for I well remember when I felt the same myself, and how long the feeling of dread and aversion towards a " papist " survived in my own breast, although my intellect had been convinced that it was unfounded and unworthy. But these feelings are not to be nursed and nurtured and fostered, as will be done when this anachronous and anarchic convention is held. They are to be argued and fought against until they are conquered. It is many years ago since I went through the struggle myself ; and I have ever since thought it my duty to try to bring others to the same state of mind to which by study, and observation, and reflection, I had arrived. It is for this reason I have dwelt on the strange and striking contrast between the treatment received by the Prote.stante et Dublin from the Roman Catholic Corporation here, and that received by the Roman Catkolics of Belfast, from the Protestant public bodies there. Facts are stubborn things.—Your obedient servant,
ARTITIR HOUSTON.
52, ritzwilliam-square, Dublin, June 4th, 1892.

P. 8.—1 may add that the committee, consisting of two Irish Unionists, two Nationalists, one Conservative, one Liberal, and one dissentient Liberal, struck out of the Bill the clauses giving to the Corporation of Belfast the same powers in respect o! reformatories and indus- trial schools now actually exercised by the Corporations of Dublin, Cork, and Limerick ; manifestly on the ground that their unfair dealing towards thew Catholic fellow-citizens rendered them unfit to be entrusted with powers that can be, and are, with safety entrusted to Catholic Corporations. I wonder how Sir Edward Har- land and Mr. T. W. Russell felt when pronouncing this condemnation. I have now before me a complete list of the officials employed by the Corporation of Derry. They are all Protestants, without a single exception. —A. H.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY DROWNING MYSTERY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY DROWNING MYSTERY AT RUNCORN.
A NAVVY ARIZESTEto ON SUSPICION.

The Runcorn Police early on Wednesday morn- ing arrested Joseph Vanderword, a ship canal navvy, better known as " Essex Joe," on a charge of causing the death of a woman named Sarah Ann Street, a young married woman, living apart from her husband. The circumstances are of a suspicious nature. The prisoner and the woman had been together most of the day, drinking, and were seen together in the neighbourhood of the canal about midnight. At that time Dr. Gastaldi walking to his home along the canal heard a splash in the water near the Gas works, and a stoker named Cliffe employed at those, words heard a scream, and both saw a man resembling the prisoner, who said a woman had jumped in the canal,and after pointing out the place,disappeared. lie had made no attempt to save her, and appeared entirely indifferent to the woman's fate. The circumstances detailed below, as given at the inquest, throw conskthrable light upon the affair, and it is to be hoped the police will succeed in unravelling the mystery.

div.head: INQUEST.--SHOCKING EVIDENCE.
div.p: THE INQUEST.--SHOCKING EVIDENCE.

Yesterday afternoon Mr. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest at the police court, Mr. W. H. Rogerson being foreman of the jury. The prisoner SUM also present, and Superintendent Atherton acted for the police. James Street, the husband of the deceased said he lived at Canal-street, and waft a labourer on the Ship Canal Works. The deceased was 27 years of age. He had a quarrel with her thirteen weeks ago about her conduct with the prisoner, and they separated. Eight or nine weeks ago he saw his wife in the Wheatsheaf Peer- house, Bridge-street, and she threatened to drown her- self if he did hot take her back. He took her back, and she lived with him until Monday morning, which was the last time he saw her alive.—By the Coroner : The deceased was fond of her beer, and would occasionally go on the drink for a day or two. Albert Boylin, Ship Canal labourer, half-brother to the deceased, living at the same house as the last wit- ness, said he saw the deceased near the post office about a quarter to teu. She was with the prisoner. Samuel Worrall, landlord of the Wheatsheaf, said the deceased was in and out of his house on Monday, Tues- day, and Wednesday. The prisoner was with per on nearly all occasions. They were in about twenty minutes to eleven on Wednesday night, and he refused to serve them because they were not sober. He was compelled to eject them. He had heard prisoner threaten that he would have her" bleeding life.' This was about three months ago. Samuel Cliff, 11, Rcbert-st., stoker at the Gas Works, 'said at midnight on Wednesday he was in the works. when he heard a scream, and ran to the canal side. On the way a big navvy met him and asked him " Have you a shaft or anything ? There's a woman in the cut." Witness ran back and got a lamplighter's staff,and when he got to the canal he could see nothing at all. It was moonlight. The man then walked away towards Delph Bridge. Ten minutes later a boat hook was procured, and the second time it was placed in the water, the body of the deceased was brought to the surface. He could not swear the prisoner was the man.
Edward Lavender, 20, Canal-st., said he saw the prisoner and deceased on Delph Bridge, about ten minutes to eleven. . .

......-- _ ...,.._. Charles Williams, 16, Parker-st., a waterman, said he was coming along the towing path of the canal, about three or four minutes past twelve, when he saw a man and a woman tramping steadily along. The woman was about 20 yards in front of the man. The prisoner was the man. Thomas Parkes, of Cholinotideley-place, Ship Canal labourer, said he was knocked up by Dr. Gastaldi, about a quarter-past twelve, and told there was a girl in the canal. Be jumped out of bed, and went to the canal bank in his shirt. There he met the prisoner, whom he knew as "Tom Essex," and he asked him what was the matter, and he replied, " A young woman has jumped into the canal," and he showed witness the place where she had sunk.

The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi said he spent Wednesday in Liverpool with some friends, and returned to Runcorn , by the 11.10 p.m. train from Lime-st., due to arrive at Runcorn at 11.47. Because it was a short cut to his home, he walked along the canal bank, and when near the gas works he heard a splash and then moan- ing. He ran to the place, and there saw a man who was standing apparently quite indifferent. He asked what was the matter, and the man replied " A girl has jumped in the canal," and in answer to a further question said she had done it of her own free will. The man said he could n-it swim, and as he (the witness) could not he went to the neighbouring houses and raised an alarm, and when he returned to the canal bank, a man in his shirt was drawing the body from the water. Catherine Cattle, wife of a Shin Canal watchman, said about three weeks ago the de- ceased told her she was really sick, jaded, and tired of her life, and she would as soon put an end to herself as live another moment. She said she and her husband lived such a wretched life together that she could not endure it any longer. On Friday last she saw the de- ceased at the house where she lived in Nelson-st., and she then said she should throw herself into the canal, and her husband should drag her out, as she could not endure her husband's cruelty and brutality any longer. —Supt. Atherton Did she ever say anything about being enciente? Witness replied that the deceased told her she was geing to have a baby, and it was not her husband's, but " Essex's." She also said that she was going to have a "broom-stick marriage after the holi- days. She had heard that deceased had a miscarriags last week.—P.C. Williams deposed that he helped to recover the body. There was-no sign of a struggle on the canal bank. He apprehended the prisoner at his lodgings in bed at three o'clock on Wednesday morning. In answer to the charge the prisoner said:—" At eleven o'clock last night I was along with this woman. I left her on the canal bank. She said she could not get into her own house. I said lam going home now, and I bid her good night. That is all I know about it."—Dr. McDougall said he had made a post martens examination. The woman's clothing was very wet, but did net appear to have been torn or pulled at all. There were no marks of violence on the body whatever.—After a brief consulta- tion in private the jury aecided to adjourn the inquest until Friday next,

div.head: TWO MN SMOCAIED IN A WIDNES
div.p: TWO MN SMOCAIED IN A WIDNES
SEWER.

Whilst working in a sewer on Widnes Marsh on Wethiesday, two men were overcome by the noxi- ous fumes and were suffocated, and a third, who went to their rescue, narrowly escaped sharing their fate. It appeared that Richard Chestr es and Richard Jones were employed to clean out the sewer by the Trustees of Hutchinson's estate, and they were assisted in their unpleasant occupation by a boy named Thomas Jones. About seven o'clock in the morning the boy was sent to a dredge boat with a message, and when he returned half-an-hour later, he found Chesters lying face downwards in the sewer, and near him was sitting Jones palpably unconscious from the influence of sewer gas. The calls of the boy brought sine men from West Bank Dock on the scene, and one of them named Wm. Lawton descended into the sewer and succeeded in placing a rope round the two men in order to draw them out, when he was overcome by the vas, and his com- panions on the bank with the utmost difficulty brought all three to the surface. Chesters was quite dead, and Jones died a few minutes afterwards. Dr. Hudson who had been sent for, and two constables endeavoured without avail to restore animation. Chesters, who was 50 years of age, had lived at 32 James-st., Widnes. and Jones, who was 30 years of age, at Wellington-st.' Run- corn, and the body of the former was conveyed to his , late borne arid that of Jones to the Arch Hotel. Four men met a similar fate in a sewer on the Marsh about i three years ago. INQUEST. Mr. F. A. Jones. the deputy coroner, yesterday after- noon held an inquest on the bodies, at the Arch Hotel, and evidence bearing out the above facts was given. It was stated that both men were experienced and well acquainted with the character of the work they had to do.—The jury were absent an hour considering their verdict, and then the foreman announced that they could not agree. The Coroner then adjourned the inquiry until the 21st inst., and intimated that if they could not then agree he should commit them to the Assizes and the sitting Judge would direct them.

• CAMBRIDGE MATHEMATICAL TRIPOS. --- SUCCESS OF A WARRINGTON MAN. The results of the above tripos, part-one, 1892, were issued on Friday morning. The Senior Wrangler, Mr. P. H. Cowell (Trinity), is a son of Mr. Cowell, of the Privy Council Bar. He was at the Rev. E. St. Parry's school, Stoke, Slough, before going to Eton. The Second Wrangler, F. R. Sharpe (Christ's), was born at Warrington, and educated at Manchester Grammar School. He is a scholar of his college,and a bicycle rider of great promise, who won the fifty mile road race recently. Mr. Hough, Third Wrangler (John's), is a scholar of his college. He comes from Invergordon, Ross- shire. He was at Aberdeen University. Miss G. E. Chisholm, of Girton, is the highest woman. Wrangler—viz., between 23 and 24 in order of merit.
THE CIVIL WAR IN VENEZUELA.. THREE ,DAYS HARD FIGHTING.

NEW YORE, WEDNESDAY.—The following despateh frcm Valencia, Venezuela, is published to-day by the " Herald."—The Federalists and the Revolutionists fought for three days on the prairies near here. Pre- sident Palacio's forces finally retreated in great disorder towards the city. General Crespo is massing his troops near Puerto Cabello, and the Federalists are preparing to meet him. The President's position is precarious.

says !--=‘• , Our friCinAs in Belfast who believe in the immaculate purity and toleration of the Town Connell, and the loyal minority generally, would do Well to look at a letter which was published in the" Daily Express" of Saturday; from the eminent Queen's Counsellor, Dr. Arthur Hous- ton, of Dublin. Dr. Houston has for many years been 'a firm and consistent Protestant Home Ruler, but he /3 only specially drawn into politics now by the fact that he has been selected as the Liberal Candidate for the Warrington divisien of Lancashire. In a recent speech he delivered, he contrasted the morality of the Nationalist Corporation of Dublin with some sad examples of want ..of liberality on the part of those who, 'where they aro in the majority, arc least inclined to be liberal themselves. tie can hardly have had any other place in his mind's eye at the time than the city of Ilellast—which is so notor- ious an example of the extent to which narrow minded_ ness and ctiquery can be carried in the conduct of municipal affairs that we need not trouble going into details, especially since these have been supplied recently in no limited quantity in our columns. Now, if the Dublin Corporation were at all chargeable with being actuated by religious considerations, it is not likely they could point to testimony such as that of Dr. Houston. The fact is that, if ts members were so inclined, they have splended opportuities of showing their bigotry, but the absence of any such display is proof that the bigotry does .note exist. The Dublin Corporation is as broadly tolerant as it is overwhelmingly Catholic, and, contrasting powerfully as it does with the exclusiveness of such bodies as the Town Council of Belfast, it affords a strong ground for the confidence of the Protestants of Ulster and of Ireland under a Home Rule Parliat'nent.

THE FIDLER'S FERRY TUNNEL. -- BURSTING OF' A MAIN PIPE. Yesterday a rumour of a . serious mishap at Fidler's Ferry arose but it seems the mishap °centred not in the tunnel, but by the bursting of a main pipe on Cuerdley Marsh, such as commonly occurs on the first charging of a pipe. The pipe was a special one, and will beiteplaced by a dupli- cate. Some of the water frorn'the burst pipe flowed into the tunnel, and is now being pumped out. The delivery of Vynrwy water into Prescot Reser- voir had begun when the burst took place, and it will be a few days before it can be resumed. No harm has been done to the works in the tunbel, add the accident will not effect the ultimate opening. RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN YORKSHIRE.

div.head: THREE PERSONS KILLED.
div.p: THREE PERSONS KILLED.

On Thursday afternoon a disastrous accident oc- curred on the Otley and Ilkley branch of the Midland Railway at Echolt Junction, not far from Bradford. An express from Leeds ran into a slow train travelling towards the former town. One of the carriages of the Bradford train was smashed to pieces, a nd several other carriages were overturned. The wreckage was great. Three passengers were killed, and many others seriously injured. The engine of the Leeds train was thrown upon its side.; but the driver and stoker escaped with comparatively slight injuries.

CRICKET'.
Middlesex all out 523 ; Scott (bowled) made 224. Cambridge beat Surrey by 80 runs, Kent 267 for six, Patterson made 114. Oxford beat Somerset by seven wickets.
FATAL ACCIDENT TO A FIREMAN.
Firemen were engaged on a burning buildiug at Hollo- way, yesterday, when the structure fell killing a man named Smart, and severely injuring six others.
THE ODDFELLO WS' CONFERENCE.

The Manchester Unity of Oddfellows resumed its conference at Derby yesterday, and affirmed by a large majority the principal that superannuation be permis- sive, and not compulsory. SHOOTING ACCIDENTS.

TWO SHOCKING FATALITIES. . Hannah Good, 35, a domestic servant, employed by Col. Spottiswoode, residing near Cork, was accidentally shot by the butler on Thursday night, while the latter was cleaning a rifle. She died on Thursday night. Yesterday a shocking fatality was reported from Llanarth, Cardiganshire. Two young men, named Lazarus Jones and John Davies, were handling a loaded gun on the highway at Brynwyn, when Miss Mary Owen, was passing on her way to market, and the gun exploded, the contents being discharged full in her face. The young lady died after intense suffering. The sportsmen were subsequently arreSted.

YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. , HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair shortly after three o'clock. Ting SHIP CANAL BILL.—On the motion of Mr. CALD- WELL, the standing order was suspended, and the Man- chester Snip Canal Bill, which was brought up from the House of Lords, was read a second time. SUPPLL—The House then, went into Committee of Supply on army estimates, and a long discussion took place on the recommendations of Lord Wantage's Com- mittee.
THE POISONING OF WOMEN IN
LONDON.

The Central News says the police are strengthening the evidence daily and hour by hour to connect a man already in custody with the recent poisoning of women in Lambeth and elsewhere for months past. The poison- ing of at least four women in London within the past eight months has, the Central News understands, been clearly traced. Whether or not the police get sufficient evidence to prefer a capital charge against a'certain individual still remains to be proved,but it is certain that evidence of a most startling and thrilling character has been obtained.

div.head: INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS OF MINERS.
div.p: INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS OF MINERS.

The International Congress of Miners, assembled in London on Thursday decided to recommend joint action on International questions, and to employ all legitimate means to secure just contracts and the fair treatment of persons in or about the mines. Various zules were adopted providing for the appointment of an organizing committee, the holding of an International Congress annually, and that no extraordinary congress should be called unless the subject to be considered was of national importance. Yesterday, at the International Congress of Miners, in London, the continental delegates supported resolutions in favour of an eight hours day for workers above and below ground. The English delegates submitted an amendment offering to confer with the surface men with a view to shortening their hours. Forty-five voted for the amendment and eighteen for the res•lution, but eventually the whole matter was referred to the or- ganizing committee.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

THE VOLUNTEHRS.— The Lyunn Volunteers assemb;ed at the Drill Hall, on Saturday last, and under the com- mand of Lieutenant Groves proceeded to Altrincham en route to Rhyl, where the battalion will be encamped until to-day (Saturday.) A DRUNIIHN DRIVER. —Oswald Savage of Hazel Grove, was charged before Mr. Brabaron on Monday, with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart on Saturday. The case was proved by P.C. Jones, and defendant was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

SERIOUS CHARGE.—James Cunningham, a Lymm fus- tian cutter, was charged before Mr. Brabazoo; on Tues- day, with having committed an assault upon Sarah Jane Hughes, twelve years of age, in Maltman's fields, Lymm, on Sunday last, and, secondly, with having, about the same time and place, committed an assault upon Sarah Jane Phillips, 13 years of age. He was committed to the Knutsford Sessions for trial. WRIT-MONDAY.—TIIS number of visitors to L.ymna during the Whitsuntide holidays has this year slightly increased, and the village has presented a somewhat buy aspect. Hundreds of cyclists passed through the village, m9,t 9f them makiag a short halt, in order to have a look 10und.

ACCIDENT.—On Thursday afternoon, in connection with the festirai of crowning the Band of Hope Qteen, a rather serious accident took place at Lymm. In the afternoon a lorry in which a number of children were seated passing Lymm Cross when one of the seats over- turned and threw the children on to the pavement, two girls, named Beardmoor and Winstanley from Rush Green, receiving severe bruises by the fall and crush. i " CROWNING TRH QIIEEN."—On Thursday the annual children's festival of " crowning " the Band of Hope Queen took place at Lvinak in tine weather, and in the presence of a large gathering of spectators. The scene of the festival was a field off Booth's-lane. The Sunday school children gathereci at their respective schools at Lymm and Oughtrington, and proceeded in procession to the field, where games &c., were indulged in. The "Queen " for the occasion was Jessie Clare, who was as usual, attended by a " body-guard" of juveniles. After the ceremony of "crowning " had taken place, all the children formed in procession and paraded Lymm, Rush Green and Oughtrington, accompiniel by the bands, including that of the ship "Indefatigable."

div.head: LOCAL BOARD MEETING.
div.p: LOCAL BOARD MEETING.

A meeting of the Local Board was held on Tuesday evening, when there were present—Mr. Gregson (chair- man), Messrs. Swallow, Holt, Whitelegg,Perrin, Brazen- dale, Appleton, and Macintyre, Ridgway (law clerk), Mullard (clerk), Mort (surveyor), Severs (gas manager), and Dr. Fox (medical officer). A VOTE OF CONDOLENCE.—The Chairman said that be- fore they proceeded to business, they ought to pass a resolution of condolence to the widow of the late Mr. Thomason. He moved that such a resolution be sent to the widow of their late respected member.—Mr. Apple- ton in seconding, said that the working-class of Lymm had lost a great friend in Mr. Thomason. The proposi- tion was carried. A COMPLAINT AT HEATLEY.—The Surveyor said that Mr. Smith had, on the 13th ult., removed the manure from near Mr. Underwood's residence at Heatley, but had since that time placed more manure in the same place.—The Clerk read a letter from Mr. Underwood, dated 31st May, in which he said that it was his inten- tion to attend the next Board meeting, as he wished to make a statement. With regard to the midden nuisance, he had written to the Local Governmeut Board because he thought that the Lymm Local Board were very negligent in their duties. The Chairman said that he p issed the midden the other day, and did not detect any offensive smell.— Mr. Underwood, who was called into the room, said that he had come on a very important matter. He said that his house was not drained, and he had had to disconnect the water closet. He would now ask them to adopt some means by which he could effectually drain his premises. He was quite willing to wait for the matter to be attended to, but he should like to see a start made.—The Law Clerk said that Mr. Underwood had no right to come before the Board without its permission.—Mr. Under- wood thought that it was quite right for a ratepayer to come and lay his complaints before the Board.—Dr. Fox: You made a great mistake in writing to the Local Government Board.—Mr. Underwood said he thought his action was right, as the local authority would not ' listen to his complaints.—The Law Clerk understood that Mr. Underwood was coming before the Board about the midden nuisance of Mr. Smith. All this matter was quite foreign.—Dr. Fox said that Mr. Underwood must recol- lect that a great deal had been done for him, and he ought not to be so hasty in his complaints. The Auth- ority would see what could be done in the matter.—Mr. Underwood thanked the Board, and left the room. TEE DRAINAGE OF HEATLEY.—Dr. Fox said that during the coming winter the draining of fleatley would have to be attended to, and he thought that they required an engineer to attend to the matter. There were one or two in his district who would do the work economically, The matter was left with the doctor to report and give further particulars at the next meeting. THE GRAMMAR Scuoor..—Mr. Richard Dutton and Mr. J. D. Dewhurst, governors of the Lymm Grammar School, sent in their resignations, and Mr. T. Swallow, and Mr. J. Gregson were appointed to fill the vacancies. This was all the business.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL ,QUARTER SESSICNS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER, will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 27th day of Juns instant, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the 'Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hun- dreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich and Wirral,: forming the Chester District, and the trials of all pri- seners committed from such Hundreds will take place, at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of. Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 27th day of June instant, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE COURT will be Adjourned ty the Court House, Nether Knutsford, on WEDNESDAY, the 29th day of June instant, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand 'Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arrising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committhel from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Ad- journed Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Ihinutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on Wan- ts-emir, the'29th day of June instant, at Eleven o!olock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester,'.7th June, 1892.
